#45657. Frieze Abu Dhabi’s Global Futures section to reflect the ‘turbulence and violence of our times’

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1040 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Frieze Abu Dhabi’s Global Futures section to reflect the ‘turbulence and violence of our times’

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1040 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Abdullah Al Saadi devises an alphabet from sweet potatoes; Ala Younis’s mosaics make monuments from old, nondescript buildings; Mohammed Joha assembles cardboard and textiles as collages addressing displacement.
  • Disparate as these works seem, they are being shown in dialogue with one another in the Global Futures section at Frieze Abu Dhabi, where they will be presented as unique systems of knowledge that preserve memory and lived experience.
  • Curated by Tarini Malik, the section features solo presentations by artists from a range of artistic and cultural backgrounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Abdullah Al Saadi devises an alphabet from sweet potatoes; Ala Younis’s mosaics make monuments from old, nondescript buildings; Mohammed Joha assembles cardboard and textiles as collages addressing displacement.

Disparate as these works seem, they are being shown in dialogue with one another in the Global Futures section at Frieze Abu Dhabi, where they will be presented as unique systems of knowledge that preserve memory and lived experience.

Curated by Tarini Malik, the section features solo presentations by artists from a range of artistic and cultural backgrounds. In some ways, the section builds upon conversations from other parts of the fair. Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi, for instance, will investigate historic routes of migration, trade and cultural exchange across the Indian Ocean. Global Futures appears to attempt this within a contemporary context.

Industry observers note that “The process of putting together Global Futures actually came together quite beautifully and organically,” Malik states. “We started with a number of proposals, looking at projects that felt so apt to this moment. We thought about what it means to have a fair, what it means to have this international constellation of galleries at this moment in Abu Dhabi. What are the conversations happening within the cultural sphere that are prevalent to this moment?”.

Sources indicate that with Taymour Grahne Projects, the Kuwaiti artist Ala Younis will present 11 works from her Climate Conditions series. The mosaic panels, crafted out of hand-cut stones and mounted on metal frames, depict old office buildings, municipal structures and other places in Abu Dhabi that are often overlooked. Younis first unveiled the series in her 2025 solo exhibition at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery. The project materialised after a three-year stay in the Emirati capital. Knowing the city’s propensity for rapid change, she sought to document and commemorate the structures as she saw them. In rendering their likeness in mosaics, Younis alludes to the Roman tiles that have outlasted the structures they once decorated. The title of the project refers to how the structures interact with the environment—their wood and metal bits expanding and contracting to changes in humidity and temperature.

The Mexican artist Tania Candiani, on the other hand, looks underground for a more sprawling and rhizomatic type of structure. Her Root Systems, presented by Galeria Vermelho, charts networks of plant roots in embroidery, unearthing a subterranean language with its own systems of exchange and communication.

“These projects established two very different but sort of complementary points of departure,” Malik indicates. “They look at these ideas of migration, of ecology, of transformation—shared across different temporalities and across different structures.”.

These themes, Malik states, resonate across the other presentations in Global Futures.

Recent findings suggest that through his Naked Sweet Potato series, Abdullah Al Saadi transcribes his personal engagement with the landscape of his native Khor Fakkan. Studying the different shapes and textures of sweet potatoes, the Emirati artist renders a language from the vegetable. He makes jewellery from it and he uses it to revisit his childhood, to transcribe his excursions to the UAE countryside. Where Candiani lays bare the universal language of roots, Al Saadi’s Naked Sweet Potato introduces an idiosyncratic and deeply personal lexicon to the conversation. The series includes drawings, paintings, sculptures and engravings, as well as collected materials. First shown at the UAE National Pavilion during the 2011 edition of the Venice Biennale, Naked Sweet Potato will be presented at Global Futures by Aisha Alabbar Gallery.

With Zawyeh Gallery, the Palestinian artist Mohammed Joha will exhibit No Shelter, building upon the series he is presenting at this year’s Venice Biennale (until 22 November). His canvases feature stratified layers of discarded textiles, paper and cardboard that come together as vibrant, abstracted landscapes.

The artist, who is based in France, began the series as he watched the destruction of his native Gaza from afar. His work comes as a poignant expression of heartache, the shredded materials evoking the devastation of Gaza and the forced displacement of its population. The way they come together in colourful compositions, however, simultaneously stands up against the violence, insisting on reconstruction in the face of ruin.

According to recent reports, “I looked at projects that reflected the turbulence of our times, the violence of our times,” Malik states. “Things can feel unsettled and art opens up a dialogue for us to understand one another.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Indian-born artist Arshi Irshad Ahmadzai, showing at Global Futures with the Mumbai-based gallery Chatterjee & Lal, will be showing her series Azal se Abad tak, which includes drawings and paintings on cloth. The works investigate how different cultures have articulated the concept of eternity.

The Ghanaian artist Godfried Donkor will present paintings, collages and embroidery with Gallery 1957. He draws from an eclectic range of inspirations for his works, including comic book superheroes, boxing athletes as well as mythological figures.

Finally, Marfa’ Projects will exhibit works by the Lebanese artist Seta Manoukian. A celebrated figure of the late 1960s Beirut art scene, Manoukian’s paintings are a stunning, often otherwordly depiction of life during the Lebanese Civil War. The works Manoukian produced after emigrating to Los Angeles in the late 1980s can be regarded as attempts at establishing stability and certainty in the aftermath of the conflict. These include works from her T-Shape series, which will be exhibited at the fair.

According to recent reports, “We have work from her Rose series to her Rock series, as well as one of her early more figurative paintings,” Malik states. “In a constellation of around five or six works, we’re trying to build something that feels like a journey through the life of a really iconic artist.”.

All in all, the Global Futures section, Malik indicates, seeks to draw connections between the exhibiting artists in a way that does not reduce the “specificity of where these artists are from and what they’re talking about”.

“I think we’ve chosen works together that really represent [a given] body of work by that artist in the best way possible,” Malik notes. “It was really about building shared connections […] while also thinking about how they intersect in the UAE and in this rapidly transforming city.”.

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November.

Should You Actually Add AI To That? A Four-Question Audit For Product Teams

📅 2026-11-12 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2763 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • A product team at a large health insurer wants to add AI that writes the full written determination for benefits appeals specialists.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

A product team at a large health insurer wants to add AI that writes the full written determination for benefits appeals specialists. The technology works as specified. However, the specialists stop using it, and the ones who keep using it take longer on each case than the ones who ignore it.

According to recent reports, A short evaluation with the specialists surfaces the problem fast: reading an AI-written determination carefully enough to sign it takes about as long as writing one, and the specialist also has to check for mistakes they would never have made themselves. The feature adds work to a task these people had already mastered.

Rescoping the release fixes it. A second version surfaces the policy provisions and prior decisions relevant to each appeal and leaves the writing to the specialist. The search step disappears, review time drops, and the part of the job the specialist is good at stays where it was.

The technology is identical in both versions, and the difference is which part of the task the AI handles.

Industry observers note that every interface change costs the user something before it pays anything back. They have to rebuild their picture of how the tool works, learn where things are now, and decide how far to trust what the AI hands them. Nelson Cowan’s review of working memory research (2001) put the limit at about four items held in mind at once. All three of those jobs draw on the same small supply.

An AI feature in an enterprise software setting requires more from the user than a redesigned menu, because it changes what they do all day. Hand the synthesis to an AI and the user becomes a checker. Give it the recommendation too, and the job shrinks to signing off. Either change costs user attention, and for people whose training is their standing at work, either one can feel like a demotion. For example, in one study, Sophia Ackerhans (2025) and colleagues found that physicians asked to sign AI-assisted decisions reported a more serious threat to their professional identity, and explanations of the AI’s reasoning raised both trust and that threat together.

It has been revealed that we can call that the break-even line. Returns to customers come in three forms:.

Recent findings suggest that for example, an AI-powered fraud screening tool indicates the errors-caught form at work, since the analyst reviews flags they would never have raised themselves, which costs attention, and the catch rate pays for it. That puts the feature above the break-even line.

Four questions can help your team locate the break-even line before design work starts. Each one produces a design condition the brief can act on.

These questions do not replace the build decision. Funding, strategy, and existing commitments all weigh on that, and four questions cannot see any of it.

Industry observers note that run through all four questions together, since no single question settles the glitch alone. Do it while the feature is still a proposal, before anyone sinks weeks into design. You will also need at least one person who does the task for a living, such as a loan officer, analyst, or benefits specialist. They do not have to sit in the roadmap meeting, and a short conversation tells you where the mental effort actually sits and whether the feature would help or add work.

Count everything the task asks of the user: the thinking, the clicking, and the checking they will owe once AI is involved. Fewer clicks proves nothing on its own, because a feature can cut clicks and still leave the person working harder. Write down the cost even when it goes up, since Question 2 may find a return that pays for it.

A loan officer reading 40 financial disclosures to find the three that conflict with lending policy is thinking hard, and AI that surfaces those conflicts cuts that demand directly. Compare that with typing a loan number into a tracking system, which costs a few seconds and almost no thought. Pre-filling that field relocates the cost instead of removing it, because the officer now checks what the machine entered. Conventional wisdom claims to automate the repetitive and monotonous tasks, and the pre-filled field is where that advice misfires. In this example:.

You can find the tasks worth automating by comparing total effort before and after. Count the checking the user inherits on the after side.

Who the user is matters as much as what the task is. One feature can clear the line for a junior analyst and fall short for a senior one. Hand a junior analyst an AI-drafted risk summary, and they gain a starting point they lack the pattern library to produce on their own. A senior analyst, however, reads that same summary against the analysis already formed in their head, spends four minutes doing it, and learns nothing.

Industry observers note that A finding like that tells you who to ship to. Scope the addition to the group it serves.

Compare the AI approach against the user’s current method, including the spreadsheets and workarounds they built for themselves. Genuine ambiguity is one reason AI comes out ahead when someone explores options, produces a starting point, or looks for patterns too numerous to spot by hand. Scale, speed, and consistency across a group of people doing the same job are three more. A fourth is catching what the current method reliably misses, which is how the fraud screening tool earns its place. The advantage disappears once the user has a practiced route to a known answer.

It has been revealed that for example, an HR team building a succession planning tool finds the answer running both ways inside one product. Using AI to surface internal candidates whose skill combinations nobody would think to search for wins on ambiguity and scale together, since no single right answer exists and manual review of that search space would take weeks. Drafting the notification email after someone picks a candidate loses to the method already in place. The format is familiar, the writing takes two minutes, and the person sending it holds firm opinions about tone. The candidate search earns the addition. The email draft layers an interaction onto a task that runs fine without one.

The nature of the input and the shape of the output are separate decisions. A task can hold genuine ambiguity and still call for a structured visual result instead of a conversational one. Pair this audit with a modality evaluation for the output side.

It has been revealed that every AI system makes mistakes. The question is whether your user will notice. Start with how visible the error is. Then weigh what it costs when nobody catches it, and whether the user still has the skill to catch it. Question 1 asks what checking costs. This one asks whether checking is even possible.

Sources indicate that error visibility varies enormously, and product teams tend to estimate it badly. For example, an AI trip planner that suggests a museum on the day it closes produces an invisible error, because nothing in the output looks wrong. The traveler finds out while standing outside a locked door in Tokyo. Compare that with a suggested flight that departs before the connecting flight lands, where the contradiction sits right there on the screen.

Sources indicate that automation bias makes the invisible cases worse. Raja Parasuraman and Dietrich Manzey (2010) reviewed decades of human factors research showing that people defer to automated output even when that output is wrong, across aviation, medicine, and process control. Trust climbs fast, and rarely as a conscious decision. Once it does, owners stop applying the scrutiny that would catch the mistake.

Map the error surface, meaning the ways this feature can be wrong, before design work starts. List the three likeliest error types. Rate each one on visibility to the user and consequence if it slips through. Any combination of low visibility and high consequence becomes a design requirement.

Industry observers note that show customers where the output came from and how the system produced it. That is provenance, and it is what lets trust settle at the right level. People who can see the source, the data behind it, and when it was pulled catch errors more often. Tell the traveler that a restaurant’s hours came from a page cached in March and they know what to check. A confident-sounding paragraph with no source attached leaves them guessing.

Recent findings suggest that letting the routine work go is a real benefit of adding AI. Nobody needs to protect a specialist’s ability to format a citation or an analyst’s ability to total a column by hand, and arguing to preserve skills the technology has absorbed wastes everyone’s time.

Recent findings suggest that still, the judgment that catches the machine’s mistakes stays exempt from replacement. That judgment makes every other delegation safe, and disuse degrades it like any other skill.

Research in radiology shows how fast a suggestion can override a reader’s own judgment. In a 2023 experiment, Thomas Dratsch and colleagues had 27 radiologists read mammograms alongside what they were told was an AI system (a simulation created solely for the experiment). The radiologists worked through a 10-image training set where the suggested category was always correct, then 40 more mammograms with incorrect suggestions planted in 12 of them. The result showed how incorrect AI suggestions damaged diagnostic accuracy at every experience level. The most experienced readers, averaging 15 years, assigned the correct category 82.3% of the time when the suggestion was right and 45.5% of the time when it was wrong, while the least experienced group fell from 79.7% to 19.8%. Experience softened the effect without preventing it. A year of deferring to the same system, with the judgment it replaced sitting unused, leaves a reader in a weaker position than the one these radiologists started from.

Question 3 looks at your user today. Extend the same test 12 months forward and you arrive at Question 4. Teams that answer the first and skip the second read the resulting failures as a quality problem in the model, when the cause is the human judgment they took out of daily use.

Sources indicate that ask whether this user could judge the quality of the output 12 months from now if the feature vanished tomorrow. When the answer is no, the design needs a mechanism that keeps verification skill in use. Periodic blind review works well and costs little, with the user forming a judgment before seeing what the AI produced. Rotating a share of cases off AI assistance does a similar job, as does a weekly comparison between machine output and a human-produced version.

Table 1 below gathers the four questions, the signals pointing each way, and the condition each one produces.

According to recent reports, table 1: The AI Addition Decision Matrix. Clear answers across all four questions point toward building the feature as proposed. A poor answer on Question 1 calls for a design condition or a change in scope, unless Question 2 finds a return that covers the cost. Questions 2 and 4 work the same way without that exception. A poor answer on Question 3 can stop the build.

Put the conditions in the design brief, where they become project requirements. Teams reduce AI features to yes or no because roadmap reviews demand it, and that throws away everything the audit found. A feature that answers well on Questions 1 and 2 and poorly on Question 3 proceeds only with provenance built in. Write that in on day one. Requirements that arrive at the end read as polish, and teams cut polish when timelines slip.

Let’s return to the insurer scenario from our opening. The first version of the tool fails Question 1. Writing a determination takes sustained thought, and the AI that produces the draft moves that effort into verification without reducing the total. An hour with the four questions would surface that before the first version reaches design.

Question 2 points in the same direction. Appeals determinations follow a familiar structure, and specialists reach the answer through a practiced route. The ambiguity in the task sits earlier, in finding which provisions and prior decisions apply.

Question 3 raises the stakes. A wrong determination affects someone’s medical coverage, and an error buried in fluent prose stays invisible until the next appeal arrives. That answer produces the provenance requirement in the second version, which cites the source document and retrieval date for every provision it surfaces.

Question 4 explains why the second version holds up. Specialists still write every determination, so the judgment that evaluates the retrieved material stays in daily use. Keeping version one would train specialists for a year to approve text they no longer have the practice to assess.

AI-generated meeting summaries sit inside products that millions of people open every day, and the audit reaches a different answer for them.

On Question 1, a summary removes the work of writing notes and adds the work of checking whether it attributed a decision to the right person. Total effort drops for the participant who never took notes. For the person who always took the notes and circulated them, the trade is closer, and the verification lands on them. That split is exactly what Question 1 is built to surface.

Question 2 compares the summary against someone typing while half-listening, which produces patchy notes. A summary beats that on completeness and on consistency from meeting to meeting, so the feature clears this question for most teams.

According to recent reports, A summary that assigns a commitment to the wrong person looks exactly like a correct one, and nobody rereads the transcript to check. On Question 3, low visibility and real consequence together turn into a requirement for a linked source timestamp behind every action item.

In a recent development, the feature clears Question 4, and the design needs no mechanism. Nobody loses a skill worth protecting by giving up meeting notes, and the participants keep making every decision the summary records.

Two clear answers, one segment finding, and one condition. The timestamps ship with the feature, and the habitual note-taker is the segment the team checks after launch.

You can run this before the next AI feature reaches your roadmap.

Everett Rogers (2003) called this pro-innovation bias, the assumption that new capability means progress before anyone verifies the benefit, and competitive pressure turns a rival’s announcement into an internal mandate. An hour of structured questions gives your team a way to answer that pressure.

Recent findings suggest that audit results land badly when a designer presents them as reasons the feature should not exist. The conditions are the useful output, so bring those into the product review.

In a recent development, start by naming the segment the feature serves, which makes the answer a yes for someone. Hand over the error surface as a requirement with a cost attached. A product manager can act on a request for timestamps behind every attributed decision, and nobody can act on a worry that consumers might not trust the output. Then offer the change in scope without waiting to be asked. A version that surfaces the provisions instead of writing the determination is a smaller build with a better adoption story, and that framing moves a roadmap conversation forward.

A sentence that works out loud: We think this clears the bar for junior analysts and adds a verification step for senior analysts, so we would scope it to onboarding and revisit the rest next quarter.

Sources indicate that the attention a person can spend in a working day stays fixed no matter how good your model gets. Before the next feature reaches design, write down what it will cost the person doing the work and which of the three returns pays for it. With both answers in hand, your team can walk into the roadmap review with a scope to propose.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just months after her death, a work by Yayoi Kusama set a upcoming auction record at Sotheby’s in New York, as the auction house kicked off the marquee November sales on Monday night with back-to-back auctions that brought in $378.7m (with fees). The evening also saw records for Sam Francis, Jonas Wood, Firelei Báez and Tomma Abts. Not a bad start to a week in which auction houses expect to sell as much as $2.4bn in art.

According to recent reports, kusama’s No. 3P.B. (1960) fetched $12.5m ($15m with fees), against an estimate of $10m to $15m, setting a latest auction record for the Japanese artist who died in August. One of Kusama's earliest landmark Infinity Nets series, the painting was included in a 1961 exhibition at the Whitney Museum of American Art, among the artist's earliest inclusions in an American institutional show. The work was the fifth most expensive lot in Sotheby’s The Now and Contemporary Evening auction, which brought in $224.78m ($268.7m with fees).

No. 3P.B. (1960) by Yayoi Kusuma. Courtesy Sotheby's.

The 53-lot sale, which carried a pre-sale estimate of $226.2m to $323.1m—the highest since May 2024, according to Sotheby’s—saw two works withdrawn and five unsold, including works by Ellsworth Kelly, Kerry James Marshall, Roy Lichtenstein and Keith Haring, as well as Ayrton Senna's Formula 1 car inexplicably included in the sale. While around 45% of lots hammered within their estimates, bidding was uneven.

It has been revealed that roy Lichtenstein’s Reflections on “Painter and Model” (1990) led the sale in terms of value, hammering for $22m ($24.6m with fees) against an estimate of $20m to $30m. It was followed by Willem de Kooning’s Water...Soft Banks and a Window (Untitled VIII) (1975), which fell short of its $20m low estimate, hammering for $17.1m ($20.3m with fees). Andy Warhol’s Flowers (1964) fetched $15.2m ($18.2m with fees), just above its $15m high estimate.

Sam Francis’s Towards Disappearance I (1958) sold for $15m ($17.1m with fees), at the low end of its $15m to $20m estimate, setting a new auction record for the artist. It was a case of déjà vu: the same painting had previously set Francis’s auction record when it sold in 1999.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most exciting moments of the evening came when five bidders battled for six minutes over Jeff Koons’s Bob-Tail (1991), a depiction of an Old English Sheepdog. The work ultimately hammered for $9m to a roar of applause.

Jeff Koons’s Bob-Tail (1991) Courtesy Sotheby's.

Another standout result was Salman Toor’s Lavender Boy (2019), which went for $340,000 ($435,200 with fees), more than four times its $80,000 high estimate even without buyer's premium being factored in.

According to recent reports, the evening kicked off with the single-owner sale of the collection of cable television magnate Theodore Baum and his wife Ruth. The 24-lot auction generated $90.8m ($109.9m with fees), comfortably within its $74.4m to $109m pre-sale estimate, with a 100% sell-through rate. However, one-third of the lots hammered below their low estimates, while just one-quarter exceeded their high estimates.

The top lot was Joan Mitchell’s Green Book of Barbara Guest (1965-68), which hammered for $16.2m ($19.3m with fees), among the highest results for the artist at auction, against an estimate of $12m to $18m. The Baums acquired the work in 1986 for just $65,000; including Sotheby’s fees, the winning bidder paid almost 300 times that amount.

Roy Lichtenstein's Two Paintings Sleeping Muse (Study) (1983) Courtesy Sotheby's.

It was followed by an untitled 1998 Mark Rothko painting, which fetched $15.5m ($17.7m with fees), surpassing its $10m to $15m estimate. The Baums purchased the work for $115,000 in 1983, according to Sotheby’s, meaning Monday’s buyer paid more than 150 times that amount, including fees. The third most valuable lot was Andy Warhol’s The Scream (After Munch) (1984), sold for $6.8m ($7.9m with fees) against an estimate of $4m to $6m. Together, the three works accounted for around 42% of the sale’s $91.4m hammer total.

It has been revealed that not every work met expectations. Franz Kline’s Figure (1955) recorded the largest shortfall in dollar terms, hammering for $1.8m ($2.3m with fees), against an estimate of $4m to $6m—55% below its low estimate.

After the sale, Sotheby’s said works from single-owner collections achieved $239m (with fees), making up almost 60% of the evening’s total earnings.

It has been revealed that “When your sale is the opener for a major season like this, there’s always a sense of heightened anticipation," Lucius Elliott, Sotheby's head of contemporary art marquee sales, remarked following the auction. "I think this evening’s sale did what everyone hoped it would—signaled that the market is in a great place and demand is strong. We saw real competition for coveted works, with a keen focus both on works from admired collections and for the works we specifically sought out for this sale to meet the demand we knew was there. The evening’s final tally—double that of the equivalent evening last season—says it all.”.

On Tuesday night, the New York art world's eyes will turn toward rival auction house Christie's for the 20th century auction, led by paintings with eight-figure estimates by Wassily Kandinsky, Gustav Klimt and Pablo Picasso.

#45653. Latest Update: AI Sped Up The Build: How Can Accessibility Testing Keep Up?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that andrew Chung is Chief Product Officer at Level Access, a Leader in the first Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Digital Accessibility Platforms.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that andrew Chung is Chief Product Officer at Level Access, a Leader in the first Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Digital Accessibility Platforms. Andrew leads the … More about Andrew ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences. Thank you!

Lately, I’ve been thinking and writing a lot about what AI is doing to product development, and what that means for accessibility. The thing that has my wheels turning is a finding from Level Access’s 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report. Basically: AI is helping us hit fast-forward on the build, but testing practices haven’t kept up.

We asked more than 2,500 professionals where they noticed AI was speeding up their work in the SDLC. Most remarked they noticed gains in planning (58%), design (61%), and development (51%). But QA and testing lagged behind: Only 30% said AI had sped up that stage.

It has been revealed that these results point to a two-speed workflow. AI has turbocharged design, planning, and development, while checking and validation are still running at a very different pace. This means a lot of teams are likely racing through the build, then being forced to hit the brakes the moment someone has to answer a pretty fundamental question: Is this thing actually accessible?

Accessibility has historically been treated as a QA bottleneck, and AI is pushing far more work into it, faster. If your team has already shifted left on accessibility, you’re off to a good start. But AI has reshuffled the workflow, so even proactive teams need to work out where those early checks belong now.

In a recent development, this matters because right now, the web is moving in the wrong direction. WebAIM’s latest scan of the top million home pages found that automatically detected errors per home page rose 10.1% in a year, from 51 to 56.1 per page. WebAIM cited AI-assisted coding as one possible contributing factor.

So how do we get validation out of first gear? How do we build human judgment into the workflow as AI keeps pushing the pace?

We looked at the organizations that are improving across every accessibility metric they track (a group we call the “improvers”) to find out what they’re doing differently.

Here’s what stood out: AI adoption made the smallest difference of anything we measured. Improvers use AI at a similar rate to everyone else we surveyed. Their edge shows up in the maturity of their surrounding accessibility practices — things like training, communication, and a culture of accessibility.

A quick caveat: This is survey data, so it only shows correlation, and mature programs may simply be better at tracking and reporting their wins. Even so, this finding was hard to ignore.

And it got even more interesting. Professionals in mature accessibility programs were nearly six times as likely to say AI helps them prioritize complications. They were also nearly three times as likely to say it helps them tackle accessibility more proactively in development.

Recent findings suggest that in other words, AI works best as an amplifier of a strong program. With context, testing, environments, and guardrails in place, agents can take on a large share of the work from drafting through to operations, and much of the time lost to waiting and handoffs goes away. People stay responsible for deciding what to build and for approving what ships.

So let me ask you: When it comes to accessibility, where does human judgment sit in your workflow today?

Not sure? Here’s a quick way to find out.

Pick a feature you shipped recently and trace it from the first Figma frame to production. Mark every moment a person decided whether it would work for someone using a keyboard, a screen reader, or their browser at 400% zoom.

Recent findings suggest that how many marks did you get? If most of them cluster at the end of creation, you’re likely heading to one of two places: You’ll either ship accessibility barriers or spend the time you saved upstream fixing them later, when they’re harder and costlier to fix.

Here’s how to avoid both outcomes by building the right accessibility checks and judgment calls into the work your team is already doing.

Industry observers note that as AI takes on more work, people need to stay involved at three points: finding issues, fixing them, and documenting the evidence. Each one plugs into a step your team already takes, like a handoff, a pull request, or a review, so nothing upcoming gets added to the timeline, and accessibility keeps pace with the work that’s in motion.

Context fades fast. Put the first judgment checkpoints as close to the creation work as you can:.

Sources indicate that found the issue? Great. Fix it while it’s fresh. When challenges end up as tickets, make sure the context travels with them. They should carry the element, the repro, the related WCAG criterion, a suggested fix, and the PR link, so context doesn’t leak.

The worst time to start gathering evidence is when somebody’s asking for it.

Industry observers note that every check, fix, and judgment call throughout the process described above should ideally leave a trail. A fix isn’t done until something fails if the problem comes back. Ask your AI assistant to write the regression test with the fix and put the finding link and any judgment call in the PR description. That’s the receipt.

It has been revealed that A passing test reveals a known glitch hasn’t returned. It doesn’t show the experience works. For what automation can’t cover, add a short note to the PR: what you tested, with which assistive technology, and any judgment calls you made.

Sources indicate that AI has given digital creation a speed boost, but broadly speaking, validating the work hasn’t kept pace. Closing that gap isn’t about adopting more AI in more places or abandoning the toolset that helped make your team faster.

According to our data, the opportunity in front of teams is to build the practice around that toolset, so that human judgment is flagged, embedded, and acted on earlier, and more often.

We’ve only scratched the surface of what our data tells us about AI and accessibility. If you’re curious about what else we found, check out the 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report. There’s plenty more to unpack.

Industry observers note that AI is changing how we design and build, and it isn’t slowing down. On December 1, 2026, SmashingConf is hosting the AI 2027 Conference, a live online half day event to take stock of where AI stands today, what we can expect in 2027, and where teams are getting it right.

With AI maturing, it’s clear we need to learn how AI can elevate your workflow as a UX designer and Design System engineer. Most of us are still figuring it out and trying to work smarter in this upcoming world, so we invited industry experts who have been doing this for a while. They show their experience and tell you what works and what doesn’t, so you don’t have to figure it all out yourself.

Recent findings suggest that every session is practical. Speakers show how they actually work: their tools, their setups, and the small things that are easy to miss. The event ends with moderated breakout rooms, where you can bring your own workflow questions. See you there?

This conference is dedicated to designers and engineers (front-end, UI, UX) who want to understand how AI can improve the way their team works, without the hype. If you’re interested in AI-ready design systems, AI and Figma, harness engineering, agentic AI UX patterns, and AI workflows for design and engineering teams, this conference is right up your alley!

Showing, not telling: All sessions will be highly practical, focusing on how to integrate AI in your daily work and what to expect in 2027.

It has been revealed that for our AI 2027 Conference, your friendly host Vitaly will welcome you and swiftly explain how the event will run. We can’t wait to meet you!

According to recent reports, AI is moving fast. With it come latest workflows in product teams, new design patterns, new user expectations and new ways of thinking about building and designing for AI.Let’s look at where things stand today. A lot changed in 2026, and there are things we can now design and build that simply weren’t possible a year ago. We’ll cover the patterns taking shape heading into 2027, from multi-modal experiences to accessibility, and what tends to go wrong along the way. A major part of that is designing for trust, so people feel confident using what we make.What makes AI products reliable in practice? We’ll look at how teams cut down on hallucinations with better context, a well-built harness and sensible guardrails. Then we’ll finish with what’s coming in 2027, including new experiments, regulations and a few takeaways to bring back to your team.Roll up your sleeves for a packed session, full of real-life examples and design patterns.

Sources indicate that great AI-powered products live at the intersection of engineering depth, design craft and product thinking. In this talk, Anna Arteeva indicates how to build real, working AI experiences, not just one-shot prototypes that fall apart the moment someone uses them.You’ll learn how to design and prototype an AI-powered experience from scratch, with functionality built on LLMs, voice and image generation logic. Anna will also show how to add that little bit of delight to your app, and how it can respond to different types of input, whatever the person on the other side of the screen gives you: text, voice or images.

Sources indicate that what coding agents need from your design system docs, and how to write it.Documentation is the part of the design system teams are least happy with, and it’s been that way for years. Luke Murphy looks at how we ended up with docs nobody reads and why agents change the picture. Then, drawing on DS ARC’s tests of real design systems, he walks through the small writing changes that make docs work for agents and people alike.This is a talk from our friends at zeroheight. Thank you for joining in!

It has been revealed that the major question for many teams is how to get your code and your Figma file talking to each other. In this session, Christine Vallaure shares how she has set this up in practice: going from code to Figma instead of the other way around, moving back and forth between the two for the best result, and what that means for how we work.You’ll hear why design system basics suddenly matter a lot more, why naming things well pays off, and why AI builders so often produce code that looks like your design system but still has to be rebuilt. She’ll also explain the engineering side that designers don’t always see, like the checks and files your developers set up, so you know how it works and what to ask for. Along the way, she covers the problems you’re likely to run into, what to keep in mind, and where Storybook fits in.Expect plenty of small tips and tricks you can take straight back to your team.

AI flipped the script on the traditional, linear design system workflow. That’s okay. We’re all experimenting, and nobody has this figured out yet.TJ Pitre has spent the past two years working with dozens of teams to find the flow that fits them. He’ll show three alternative workflows live. Which one fits depends on you: how major your design system is, how big your team is, how much effort you’re willing to put in, and how well it needs to scale.The goal is to get you thinking, and to send you back to your team with a few workflows worth trying.

Recent findings suggest that brad Frost shares his actual workflow for building products with AI and a design system. He’ll show the setup, architecture, and tools he uses to keep AI on the rails of his components, tokens, and patterns.Expect live building, real design decisions, and plenty of practical tricks along the way. You’ll see how it all works together and leave with ideas to apply to your own design system and workflow.

Meshfont is a free browser font editor that lets you sculpt open-licensed typefaces with BÃ©zier handles, warp tools, and MCP AI agents.

In a recent development, open the Meshfont homepage and the interface behaves like a live drafting table. Hairline rulers frame the top and left edges, while thin red alignment guides cut across the baseline and x-height behind an oversized blue lowercase âa.â Right above that glyph, two compact switches set the tone for the whole tool: a script toggle between Latin and Japanese characters, and a mode pill flipping between Warp and BÃ©zier editing. You don't have to install desktop software or hunt for a buried toolbar to start pulling anchor points.

Jump into the dark-mode workspace and Meshfont avoids the intimidation of an empty artboard. A clean modal asks how you want to begin, offering eight open-licensed starting points: Inter, Playfair, Outfit, Space Grotesk, Varela Round, JetBrains Mono, Japanese kana, and Mincho. Signed-in users can also import a.ttf or.otf file or start from scratch. Behind that picker, a color-coded virtual keyboard anchors the bottom of the screen beneath a dotted glyph canvas, making character switching fast and tactile.

The clearest sign of where this browser font editor is heading sits on its AI agents page. Meshfont lets you connect Claude, Claude Code, Cursor, or Codex directly through MCP so an assistant can read your existing outlines, spacing, and kerning. Draw a handful of letters yourself, and the agent drafts missing characters in your style as proposals you can keep or decline. It's a practical division of labor: you set the formal rules, and the tool handles the repetitive glyph expansion.

Even the sign-in screen reinforces that playful typographic energy. A quiet dark email panel sits beside tilted specimen cards featuring a cobalt-blue serif âAa,â a crisp ampersand on charcoal, and layered outlined âgâ forms on lime. Everything in this browser font editor stays focused on getting designers from a rough curve to an exportable font without friction.

#45641. Do art fairs care about non-VIP visitors?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1418 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Do art fairs care about non-VIP visitors?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1418 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • October’s Paris art week had become the must-attend fixture of the international art market calendar, particularly for wealthy Americans.
  • “It’s important to be in Paris,” remarked Chris Sharp, the Los Angeles gallerist and founder of Post-Fair, a boutique California-based event that held its first edition in the French capital this October.
  • The previous weekend, Paris had been rocked by mass demonstrations that in some areas had escalated into riots and looting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

October’s Paris art week had become the must-attend fixture of the international art market calendar, particularly for wealthy Americans. No other city could match the range and quality of the French capital’s art fairs and exhibitions, both at public museums and private foundations. And what about all those charming restaurants, cafes and shops?

“It’s important to be in Paris,” remarked Chris Sharp, the Los Angeles gallerist and founder of Post-Fair, a boutique California-based event that held its first edition in the French capital this October. “Paris is the undisputed capital of the art world—once a year,” Sharp added, speaking at Post-Fair’s preview on 19 October, in the chic Marais district. Nearby, someone had sprayed “mort aux riches” across the window of a bank.

The previous weekend, Paris had been rocked by mass demonstrations that in some areas had escalated into riots and looting. Further demonstrations, highlighting the neglected state of France’s secondary schools, the ever-rising cost of living and other grievances, had been planned in Paris and other French cities on the afternoon of Saturday 24 October. Unemployment in France for those aged 15 to 24 at the moment stands at 21.5%, almost three times the rate in neighbouring Germany.

On Tuesday 20 October, the day of the ultra-exclusive Avant-Première pre-preview of Art Basel Paris in the Grand Palais, the French activist collective Pillage de Classe (class plunder) posted a message on Instagram exhorting protesters to “take back” the famous Belle Époque exhibition hall on Saturday, the penultimate day of the week’s flagship fair.

Art Basel Paris has been held in the historic Grand Palais since 2024.

It has been revealed that of course, the Grand Palais was not stormed, Bastille-style. In the highly unlikely event of protesters managing to “take back” the building, they would have been disappointed, just as revolutionaries had been in 1789, when they discovered the prison they had liberated contained just seven detainees. Art Basel Paris, taking no risks, had closed the event two days early on Friday evening (after an excoriating letter from France's gallery association to fair director Karim Crippa, Art Basel recompensed exhibitors 20% of their stand fees).

Industry observers note that the mega-gallery Hauser & Wirth took even fewer risks, emptying its stand the day before, leaving three paintings by the local artist Hélène Delprat. The fair had been shortened to three VIP preview days plus just one day for the general public. Satellite fairs, like Paris Internationale and Post-Fair, closed at lunchtime on Saturday.

Recent findings suggest that that Saturday afternoon, more than 100,000 people duly turned out to demonstrate. However, these proved predominantly peaceful and were confined by the police to the outskirts of the city.

Recent findings suggest that the disruption in Paris had surely been a momentary blip. And Art Basel’s ultra-wealthy invitees, which the top end of the international art trade likes to call the “right kind of people”, had already been and gone. But what about the reputational impact?

“The collateral damage is substantial considering the whole point of being in Paris is to let yourself surrender to its myriad charms,” said Andrew Terner, a Latest York-based private dealer and collector, speaking in the immediate aftermath of the early closure.

The French authorities blamed “ultra-left radical groups” for the violence that had marred weeks of otherwise peaceful protests, begun in September by discontented teenage lycée students. Pillage de Classe is certainly a left-wing radical group; it views Art Basel Paris as a luxury playground in which art is used by the ultra-wealthy to protect their capital from taxation.

In a recent development, but maybe (leaving aside its desire to take the Grand Palais by storm) Pillage de Classe has a point, at least with regard to the fair’s top French clients. In France, the net worth of the country’s 500 wealthiest individuals has ballooned from 6% of the country’s GDP in 1996 to 42% in 2024, according to a much-cited article in the French business magazine Challenges. Tax reforms introduced by President Macron in 2017 excluded stocks, financial assets (including art) and corporate investments from wealth tax calculations.

Moreover, in 2003 the French government had granted tax breaks of up to 75% for private individuals and 60% for corporations that supported the arts. This encouraged investment in glitzy private foundations, such as the Fondation Louis Vuitton, François Pinault’s Bourse de Commerce, the Fondation Cartier and the newly opened Île Seguin luxury hotel and Large art centre, which have become such an alluring feature of the Paris art scene for international visitors. According to research by Apollo magazine, Bernard Arnault’s LVMH luxury group received an aggregate tax break of €518.1m between 2007 and 2017 to set against the €790m the corporation spent building the Frank Gehry-designed Fondation Louis Vuitton.

In a recent development, the ultra-wealthy have also grown a lot wealthier in the US in recent years. The share of the nation’s wealth held by the richest 0.0001% (around 200 individuals) is now more than seven times what it was in 1980, according to a November Substack posted by the Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman.

Today’s art market is dominated by the world’s wealthiest people buying the world’s most expensive art. Most of these people are pretty old. This is not a good look now that the Democrats have won a landslide victory in the US midterm elections, driven by a massive turnout of young voters. Authoritarian rulers like Viktor Orbán in Hungary and Aleksandar Vučić in Serbia have been voted out of office. Young people have been protesting en masse about their diminished life chances in France and more than a dozen other countries across the world.

Suddenly, ordinary people matter again. The young matter. But do they matter at art fairs?

Take ticket-pricing. In October, the general public were charged £48 each to attend Frieze London, with students being asked to pay £32. Does Frieze, which is owned by the billionaire Ari Emanuel, the former chief executive of the US entertainment conglomerate Endeavor, want to actively discourage young people from visiting? Or is that ticket price an acknowledgement that pretty much the only students who can now afford to attend the UK’s art colleges come from more affluent backgrounds?

Industry observers note that the following week, Art Basel Paris, part of James Murdoch’s Lupa Systems investment portfolio, was charging €47 for a standard day pass and €30 for a student ticket. “The galleries pay for the fair. Visitors are a side business,” says Magnus Resch, a Fresh York-based author and art market entrepreneur. According to Resch’s back-of-an-envelope calculations, stand fees generate at least €15m, while tickets bring in less than €3m. “Charging the public €47 isn’t about the money. It’s about keeping the fair exclusive.” (Art Basel does not reveal detailed breakdowns of its revenue streams.).

According to recent reports, “It is crucial for the public to visit an art fair,” says Guillaume Sultana, whose contemporary art gallery exhibited on the upper level of Art Basel Paris, where footfall is slower than down on the ground floor among the mega-galleries. “But a lot of general visitors on the weekend are a bit frustrated because public tickets are very expensive.”.

Recent findings suggest that sultana acknowledges that “the main business is done during the very first days of an art fair, always”. Despite the fair being truncated, Sultana describes the experience as “very good”, having sold a painting by the young Syrian artist Osama Al Rayyan during the preview for €15,000, among other works.

According to recent reports, in the funfair-mirror optics of the international art market, €15,000 might appear a relatively “affordable” price point. But traditionally, sensible collectors have been advised to spend no more than 5% of their available wealth on art. So, whoever bought that Al Rayan painting, should, theoretically, have had €300,000 of spare cash available. For would-be younger collectors in today’s tough economic conditions, these are intimidating figures, unless they can call on the bank of mum and dad.

It has been revealed that collecting art is in serious danger of being perceived as something that old, rich people do. With so many established collectors ageing and selling, rather than buying, and a democratic wave pushing back against oligarchical wealth, this might be a good moment for the art market to think more about inclusivity than exclusivity, to take a broader view of who might be the “right kind” of people.

After all, who wants “death to the rich” sprayed across their gallery window?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • ThreeRT by MeshyAI brings real-time ray tracing at 60 fps to a three.js-style API, trading baked shadow maps for live bounce light.
  • Industry observers note that dragging the comparison sliders on ThreeRT makes the gap between rasterization and path tracing obvious within seconds.
  • According to recent reports, the Zero-Day sci-fi corridor highlights an even sharper split when you scrub the camera timeline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ThreeRT by MeshyAI brings real-time ray tracing at 60 fps to a three.js-style API, trading baked shadow maps for live bounce light.

Industry observers note that dragging the comparison sliders on ThreeRT makes the gap between rasterization and path tracing obvious within seconds. In the Bistro night scene, standard three.js under WebGL leaves the cobblestones cool and flat, with a blown-out white hotspot around the round shop sign. Even with WebGPU and SSGI turned on, the lamp glare stays harsh and the pavement loses multi-bounce warmth. Slide the divider across to ThreeRT, and warm golden light spills from the shop window across the facade while overhead string lights tint the street in their own colors.

According to recent reports, the Zero-Day sci-fi corridor highlights an even sharper split when you scrub the camera timeline. On the three.js side, ceiling pipes and glossy floors pick up heavy speckle noise, and unlit industrial housings sink into dark blue shadows. ThreeRT keeps those white and grey panels legible through soft indirect bounce light from tiny amber emitters. It doesn't rely on light probes or baked maps, so moving the camera at 60 fps never breaks the reflections of off-screen geometry.

Recent findings suggest that that matters for the future of ray tracing in the browser. Today, ThreeRT runs its Rust and wgpu path tracer inside a native client while exposing a familiar three.js-style TypeScript API. The same scene code still runs as plain three.js in any browser or WebView, which gives developers one codebase across both worlds. As WebGPU hardware ray tracing matures on the web, that gap is closing fast.

You can see the range in the project gallery, from the OpenStrikeRT foundry hall where a furnace lights the surrounding concrete, to smaller studies like Jeweller's Window, Daylight Home, and Boutique Showroom. Each surface reacts to real emitters instead of faked ambient fill. See the full project on ThreeRTâs website.

Tech Report: MCA Chicago receives gift of 65 works, most of them by women and artists of colour

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A recent gift of 65 works to the Museum of Contemporary Art (MCA) Chicago honours the institution's upcoming 60th anniversary and its outgoing director, Madeleine Grynsztejn.
  • The philanthropists Jack and Sandy Guthman worked with the MCA’s curatorial team, poring through the couple’s extensive collection to choose the pieces.
  • Grynsztejn considers this an extraordinary model for what can happen when a museum and philanthropists are in alignment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A recent gift of 65 works to the Museum of Contemporary Art (MCA) Chicago honours the institution's upcoming 60th anniversary and its outgoing director, Madeleine Grynsztejn.

The philanthropists Jack and Sandy Guthman worked with the MCA’s curatorial team, poring through the couple’s extensive collection to choose the pieces. Grynsztejn got the selection down to 65, then hit a wall. Paring it down to 60, as originally intended, became an excruciating process. The Guthmans, champions of the MCA for decades, did not force the museum to choose just 60.

Grynsztejn considers this an extraordinary model for what can happen when a museum and philanthropists are in alignment. To date, the Guthmans have donated 130 works to the MCA—the largest donor gift in the museum’s history.

In a recent development, for Grynsztejn, building a great museum collection takes not only visionary leadership but visionary philanthropy. “The Guthmans have invested in Chicago artists, making their gift one that also has a civic impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. Included in the gift is work by Amanda Williams, Dawoud Bey and Rashid Johnson.

According to recent reports, the Guthmans have spent decades supporting Chicago’s civic and cultural institutions. As a real estate lawyer, Jack started out by providing pro bono services. Meanwhile, Sandy directed her family’s foundation Polk Bros. Jack was elected as a trustee of the MCA in 1989 and currently serves on its board. For the MCA’s 50th anniversary, the couple donated 50 photographs by women artists.

Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995–96) Photo: Nathan Keay, © MCA Chicago.

Industry observers note that the current gift includes 23 pieces by artists of colour and 19 by women. Thirteen artists are fresh to the MCA’s collection, including Mohamed Bourouissa, James Casebere, Julia Fish, Christian Marclay, Adrian Paci, Elle Perez and Shinique Smith. Other gifts, like photographs by Bey, deepen the MCA’s holdings.

“In some cases, we are adding an entirely latest collection,” Grynsztejn says, referring to Bey’s early photography in Harlem, “and in some cases, we are gaining an icon, as in Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995-96).”.

The MCA began as a kunsthalle in 1967. It started receiving gifts, so in 1974 it formalised its collection. Despite the fact that the very first piece to enter the MCA’s collection was by Marisol, it eventually began to reflect the usual gender and racial biases.

During her tenure, Grynsztejn has sought to change that by establishing the Women Artists Initiative, inspired by the experience of many colleagues who have found it more challenging to fundraise for exhibitions by women artists. The museum’s proof-of-concept came with the success of exhibitions by Faith Ringgold, followed by a traveling Yoko Ono retrospective. The MCA has added women artists to the collection at four times the national average. Recently, the initiative has been renamed the Madeleine Fund for Women Artists and now has a $5m endowment.

Since Grynsztejn’s arrival at the museum in 2008, the MCA’s collection has grown from approximately 1,300 to 3,800 works. At least half of the acquisitions under her leadership have been by women and artists of colour. “This is not woke or [diversity, equity and inclusion],” she claims. “It’s good business and good culture. Because if you are a public trust, you are in service to your public.”.

BIG reveals "modular blueprint" for Refugee City in Uganda

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (482 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architecture studio MAJOR has unveiled plans for Refugee City, a masterplan that reimagines the Bidi Bidi refugee settlement in Uganda as an economic hub.
  • Developed by SIGNIFICANT in collaboration with social enterprise To.org, the masterplan proposes essential civic infrastructure such as housing, schools and markets for the largest refugee settlement in Africa, home to around 250,000 displaced people.
  • The initiative was conceptualised as an alternative to short-term aid and charity-led approaches to refugee settlements, providing a “resilient economic model” that empowers displaced communities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Architecture studio MAJOR has unveiled plans for Refugee City, a masterplan that reimagines the Bidi Bidi refugee settlement in Uganda as an economic hub.

Developed by SIGNIFICANT in collaboration with social enterprise To.org, the masterplan proposes essential civic infrastructure such as housing, schools and markets for the largest refugee settlement in Africa, home to around 250,000 displaced people.

The initiative was conceptualised as an alternative to short-term aid and charity-led approaches to refugee settlements, providing a “resilient economic model” that empowers displaced communities.

“If the average stay in refugee camps is around two decades, then the term temporary cannot be noted to suffice,” said studio founder Bjarke Ingels.

“If we start thinking of cities rather than camps, then charity becomes investments into the future, and if companies can be incentivised to locate their production in refugee cities, then the refugees can be given economic opportunities that they presently long for.”.

If completed, the project would sit alongside an existing performing arts centre completed on the site in 2024.

The masterplan is designed by SUBSTANTIAL to be “scalable and modular” to facilitate its implementation in other locations.

“We have attempted to design a scalable, phaseable, modular blueprint for a upcoming way to accommodate the global flow of refugees,” Ingels noted.

In a bid to allow the city to grow organically, the proposal takes a “fractal approach” – beginning with the establishment of housing units before expanding to neighbourhoods and eventually districts over several years.

According to recent reports, the first phase of the project comprises a prototype single-family housing unit, which is currently being built on the site. Its modular structure was designed to improve existing shelter typologies, while also drawing on local buildings.

Once complete, the unit will function as an operational guesthouse to accommodate international investors and future collaborators on the site.

“The prototype base unit is inspired by local vernacular settlements where homes grow as a sequence of rooms around shared spaces,” To.org co-founder Nachson Mimran told Dezeen.

Renders of the city reveal designs for a commercial street lined with markets and built from local materials such as brick and bamboo.

The Bidi Bidi settlement in Uganda was chosen as the site for the inaugural Refugee City because of the country’s 2006 Refugee Act, which grants refugees the right to work and start businesses, freedom of movement, and to acquire agricultural plots within integrated rural settlements.

“There are very few nations offering this unique combination which makes Uganda the ideal location for the inaugural Refugee City,” Mimran remarked.

The realisation of the full-scale masterplan in Bidi Bidi is dependent on capital investment, while any future initiatives will require host-nation governments to be willing to grant flexibility and legal work rights to refugees.

Other spaces designed for refugees include an easy-build playground for children fleeing war, and wooden refugee beds designed to provide more privacy and dignity.

Polestar Formula 2030 concept car "screams performance"

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (717 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Swedish electric-vehicle brand Polestar has unveiled the Formula 2030 concept car featuring interchangeable, customisable dashboard buttons.
  • The first Polestar concept created under the direction of head of design Philipp Römers, the Formula 2030 is intended to herald the design direction of the firm’s production cars in the coming years.
  • It takes the form of a low-slung sports car with proportions that Römers mentioned “scream performance”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Swedish electric-vehicle brand Polestar has unveiled the Formula 2030 concept car featuring interchangeable, customisable dashboard buttons.

The first Polestar concept created under the direction of head of design Philipp Römers, the Formula 2030 is intended to herald the design direction of the firm’s production cars in the coming years.

It takes the form of a low-slung sports car with proportions that Römers mentioned “scream performance”.

With signature “Dual Blade” headlights, the front of the car previews the face of the next-generation Polestar 2, a saloon scheduled to launch in 2027.

Meanwhile, the tail of the Formula 2030 mirrors the upcoming Polestar 7 crossover SUV, moving away from the continuous rear lightbar that has become widespread among electric cars in favour of separate “Single Blade” lights.

Unlike Polestar’s most recently released production vehicles, the Polestar 4 and Polestar 5, the Formula 2030 also has a conventional rear windscreen.

“Design should always reflect the values and mission of a brand and that is exactly what we did with Polestar Formula 2030 concept,” mentioned Römers, who joined Polestar from Audi in January 2025.

“It is a physical embodiment of how we apply Polestar’s core values of design, performance and sustainability to the next production cars.”.

At 1.35 metres tall, 4.68 metres long and 2.02 metres wide, the Formula 2030 has a very low roofline but a broad stance.

Its styling was intended to project power, with a long bonnet, wraparound windscreen, short overhangs, muscular haunches and substantial 22-inch wheels.

Other sporty design elements include a deep front splitter and a single vertical windscreen wiper.

The Formula 2030 showcases a newly developed paint colour called Nitrogen, with accents of gold dotted throughout the car.

Inside, the design echoes efforts in recent concept cars from other carmakers to emphasise the driving experience.

The cockpit features a curved screen band mounted above the steering wheel, presenting information to the driver.

Another screen is integrated into the centre console, which slopes gently up to the dashboard.

A sliding “drive mode selector” on the centre console would allow the car to alternate between three modes – Performance, Normal and Autonomous – changing the angle of the central screen, seating and steering wheel to allow for a more passive or active driving position.

The Formula 2030 embraces a wider trend in car design back towards incorporating physical buttons, rather than only touchscreens.

In a recent development, also occupying the central console is an interface of eight large mechanical controls. These can be configured to the user’s preferences, with choices between different types of buttons and switches capable of being programmed for specific functions.

In a modest nod to sustainability, the seat backs are made from a bio-based composite combining European flax and bio-based polypropylene, while the insides of the doors are made from a single material in order to be recyclable.

Headquartered in Gothenburg, Polestar has emphasised design and sustainability since it was spun out of Volvo as a premium EV brand in 2017.

According to recent reports, amid heavy financial losses, it has increased its production of SUVs, which tend to be popular with consumers and deliver higher profit margins. SUVs or SUV-adjacent cars now account for three of the five models in its lineup.

SUVs are often associated with a greater environmental impact than other types of cars, but Polestar denies watering down its ambitions on sustainability.

According to its most recent sustainability report, published in April, the firm is ahead of schedule on a target to halve greenhouse-gas emissions per vehicle sold between 2020 and 2030.

Industry observers note that it is the only car brand that publishes life-cycle carbon assessments for all its models. Assessments for the upcoming Polestar 2 and Polestar 7 have not yet been calculated.

“Learnings from the cars we have already produced will be channelled into the new cars to bring the CO2e figures in as low as possible,” a spokesperson told Dezeen.

In a recent development, in 2021, Polestar revealed a project to produce a “truly climate-neutral car” by 2030. Earlier this year, it pushed this target back to 2035 owing to the “scale and complexity of the challenge”.

Other concept cars recently covered on Dezeen include the flying Tesla Roadster and a Fiat that transforms from an SUV into a pickup truck.

The cost of a will varies dramatically based on how you create it and how complex your estate is. Here is a comprehensive comparison of every method, from free options to premium attorney packages.

Several factors push will costs toward the higher end of each range:.

The will vs trust decision is primarily a financial calculation: does the upfront cost of a trust save more than it costs by avoiding probate?

Sources indicate that when you die with only a will (no trust), your estate must go through probate — a court-supervised process where a judge validates your will, your executor inventories assets, debts are paid, and remaining assets are distributed. Probate costs include:.

Probate also takes 6-18 months on average and is a public proceeding — anyone can look up your will, your assets, and who inherited what.

Recent findings suggest that A revocable living trust costs $1,500-$5,000 upfront but avoids probate entirely. The math is straightforward:.

Recent findings suggest that for most FI-focused households who are building wealth toward financial independence, the trust pays for itself many times over. If your net worth exceeds $100,000-$200,000 and you own real estate, a trust is almost certainly the better financial decision.

According to recent reports, even with a trust, you still need a pour-over will — a short document that catches any assets not transferred into the trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. You also still need a healthcare directive and durable power of attorney. Most estate initiative packages include all four documents together.

Sources indicate that the sticker price of a will is only part of the total cost of estate planning. Several hidden costs catch people off guard:.

The FI-optimized approach to estate planning minimizes cost without sacrificing protection:.

Start with an online will now. A $159 Trust & Will plan gives you a will, healthcare directive, and power of attorney today. Do not let perfect be the enemy of done — having a basic will is infinitely better than having no will while you save up for an attorney.

Upgrade to a trust when your net worth exceeds $200,000. At this point, the probate avoidance savings justify the $1,500-$3,500 cost of adding a trust.

It has been revealed that shop attorney fees aggressively. Estate planning is a competitive market. Get quotes from at least three attorneys. Many offer flat-fee packages, and prices can vary by 50-100% for the same work in the same city. Ask specifically whether the quote includes trust funding assistance and deed transfers.

Recent findings suggest that use online services for updates. Rather than paying an attorney $200-$500 for a codicil, many online platforms let you revision your will for free or for a small annual subscription ($19-$39/year). Trust & Will, for example, includes one year of free updates.

Bundle documents. An estate strategy package (will + trust + POA + healthcare directive) typically costs 20-40% less than purchasing each document separately. If you are going to see an attorney, get everything done in one engagement.

According to recent reports, here is the counterintuitive truth: the most expensive estate initiative is the one you never create. Dying without a will (intestate) triggers state default rules that may not match your wishes, longer and more expensive probate proceedings, and potential family conflict. For parents of minor children, it means a judge — not you — decides who raises your kids. The $0-$259 cost of an online will is trivially small compared to these consequences.

If your net worth exceeds $200,000, a $2,000-$3,500 revocable living trust saves your family $10,000-$35,000 or more in probate costs and 6-18 months of waiting. That is a 300-1,000% return on a one-time investment. For anyone on the path to financial independence, this is one of the highest-ROI financial moves you can make. The trust also provides privacy (wills are public, trusts are not), seamless incapacity planning, and immediate asset distribution to your beneficiaries without court involvement.

Industry observers note that yes. FreeWill (freewill.com) offers a free basic will funded by nonprofit partners. Some states also accept handwritten (holographic) wills that cost nothing. Military personnel can get free wills through the JAG office on any military installation. Many bar associations and legal aid societies offer free will clinics several times per year. While these free options work for simple estates, you may want to pay $99-$259 for a more comprehensive online service that includes healthcare directives and power of attorney.

Attorneys charge $300-$750 for a simple will and $750-$1,500 for a complex will with special provisions. A complete estate blueprint package (will, trust, power of attorney, healthcare directive) runs $1,500-$5,000. Fees vary significantly by location — attorneys in major metros charge 2-3 times more than attorneys in smaller cities for the same work. Always ask for a flat fee rather than hourly billing for estate planning.

For straightforward estates, yes. Major online will makers like Trust & Will, Nolo WillMaker, and LegalZoom produce documents that are legally valid in all 50 states and cover the same core elements an attorney would include. The difference is that an attorney can provide customized advice, handle complex situations, and anticipate challenges specific to your state law. If your estate is simple, an online will is functionally equivalent. If your situation has any complexity, the attorney consultation is worth the additional cost.

Online services typically include free updates for one year and then charge $19-$39 per year for ongoing access. An attorney charges $100-$500 for a codicil (formal amendment) or $300-$1,000 to draft a fresh will. For minor changes, a codicil is sufficient. For major changes (new spouse, additional children, significant asset changes), creating an entirely new will is cleaner and reduces the risk of conflicting instructions.

If your estate is under $100,000-$200,000 with no real estate, a will alone is often sufficient. Once your net worth exceeds $200,000 or you own real property, a revocable living trust typically saves more in probate avoidance ($15,000-$70,000 on a $500,000-$1,000,000 estate) than it costs ($1,500-$5,000). A trust also provides privacy, avoids the 6-18 month probate timeline, and manages your assets if you become incapacitated. For most FI-focused households building significant wealth, a trust is the better long-term choice.

According to recent reports, the most expensive part of estate planning is NOT the documents — it is probate. Probate costs 3-7% of your estate value ($15,000-$70,000 on a $500,000-$1,000,000 estate) and takes 6-18 months. By comparison, even the most expensive estate strategy package ($5,000-$10,000) is a fraction of what your family would spend navigating probate without a trust. The second most expensive mistake is outdated beneficiary designations on retirement accounts, which can send six or seven figures to the wrong person with no legal recourse.

It has been revealed that the cost of a will ranges from $0 to $10,000+ depending on your method and complexity, but the most expensive option is always having no will at all. For most FI-focused households, start with an online will for $0-$259 to get basic protection in place immediately. As your net worth grows beyond $200,000, invest $1,500-$5,000 in a comprehensive estate strategy with a revocable living trust — the probate savings alone deliver a 300-1,000% return. Enhancement your beneficiary designations today (free), review your plan every 3-5 years, and remember: the goal of estate planning is not to create perfect documents. It is to protect the people you love from financial chaos during the worst moment of their lives.

Four hands in ruffled lace cuffs and pink brocade sleeves reach in from the dark corners of the opening frame, crossing chrome flashlight beams over a stacked white wordmark. History didnât get toned down this year. Itâs From Formâs fifth year shaping the annual Amsterdam Museum Night, and co-founders Ashley Govers and Jurjen Versteeg dropped their earlier habit of balancing historic cues with safe modern polish. Early editions leaned on flip-books before annual resets explored time travel in 2024 and collecting in 2025. Starting from the classical musical nocturne, the Rotterdam duo recast Amsterdamâs 65-plus participating museums as an unscripted nighttime maze.

A crisp white top band locks black MUSEUM NACHT caps opposite the ZATERDAG 7 NOVEMBER 2026 date stamp, while white AMSTERDAM type drops straight into the dark scene below, linked across the border by a looping crimson line. Versteeg notes that the studio studied the elongated necks and enlarged eyes of 17th-century paintings alongside forced-perspective miniature dioramas. Inside a backlit Mupi frame, the costumed character stands in the bottom-right corner and aims a cool blue flashlight beam diagonally across black curtain folds toward the stacked title lockup, grounded by a narrow white partner strip along the base. Perforated brick walls envelop giant market in Kinshasa by Think Tank Architecture
