📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Martin Argyroglo excluding top photo by Ville Kinshasa & SZTC.
  • French studio Think Tank Architecture has created a market in the capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo, with space for 20,000 vendors across its geometric brick-and-concrete structure.
  • Named Zando Central Market, the building replaces a historic market on the same site in Kinshasa that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Martin Argyroglo excluding top photo by Ville Kinshasa & SZTC.

French studio Think Tank Architecture has created a market in the capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo, with space for 20,000 vendors across its geometric brick-and-concrete structure.

Named Zando Central Market, the building replaces a historic market on the same site in Kinshasa that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.

Think Tank Architecture was brought in to design the replacement market after the original building had already been torn down. The studio used this as an opportunity to completely reimagine the role and function of the market, while taking visual cues from the original building and others like it in the city.

Alongside an increased number of vendor stalls, the 82,000-square-metre replacement incorporates storage space, a fire station, a police station, a medical centre, a vet’s, offices and a food court.

“The newly introduced market is on the same site as the ancient one, on the 3.7-hectare plot,” Think Tank Architecture told Dezeen.

“However, the building’s footprint has been totally redefined, taking into consideration the scale of the program and the urban context,” it continued.

In a recent development, “We wanted it to be an African market, and not an interpretation of it. Our comprehension comes from academic, historic and architectural research, dialogue with the client and then visits to other markets in Kinshasa.”.

According to recent reports, zando Central Market has a rectangular initiative measuring 245 metres in length and 150 metres in width. It contains 650 shops with space for 20,000 vendors, which is “more than 5 times its original capacity”, according to the studio.

At its heart is the central covered market, spanning two double-height levels, with three large entrances and outward views used to orient visitors.

According to recent reports, it is surrounded by a three-storey building containing the other facilities. Landscaped patios punctuate the plan, carving out space for public squares and informal markets to take place.

“It’s an notable part of our approach to keep the building open to the public, including the more modest,” said Think Tank Architecture.

It has been revealed that the material palette for the project comprises brick and concrete, chosen to be in keeping with the local context and skills of the region’s construction workers. Demolition waste from the original market was used in the substructure.

“We are quite happy to say that this project reactivated three terracotta factories within a 60-kilometre distance from the market,” reflected the studio.

It uses a mushroom-slab structural system, in which the columns flare at their top, referencing the original market’s design.

Meanwhile, the perforated brick facades were designed to facilitate natural ventilation and provide shade from the sun.

In tandem with the thermal mass from the concrete, this helps cool the building, minimising the need for technical cooling equipment and keeping project costs low.

Interior finishes were also kept deliberately simple for cost reasons. However, the perforations of the facades help add flourish, evoking moucharabiehs – a type of projecting oriel window enclosed with wooden latticework, typically seen in traditional Islamic architecture.

Zando Central Market is on the eight-strong shortlist for the civic project category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, alongside projects including Sydney Fish Market by 3XN and TCC DAKA Renewable Resource Recycling Center by KPF.

It is yet to officially open, as the second phase of the project – involving the renovation of the surrounding streets – needs to be completed to allow access.

Industry observers note that “This phase of works is under the city’s supervision and is going slower,” mentioned Think Tank Architecture. “We hope, and it’s in our client’s interest, that the market will be able to open by the end of this year.”.

Other market architecture recently featured on Dezeen includes the multi-level Tepoztlán Market in central Mexico by local studios Ramírez Suarez Arquitectos and Laboratorio Regional de Arquitectura, and an open-air market in Colombia designed by Tarq Studio to accommodate community gatherings.

Photography by Martin Argyroglo excluding top photo by Ville Kinshasa & SZTC.

#45618. Parthenon’s east pediment, ‘the most famous image of antiquity’, recreated in Frankfurt exhibition

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Parthenon’s east pediment, ‘the most famous image of antiquity’, recreated in Frankfurt exhibition

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vinzenz Brinkmann’s quest to solve the mysteries of the destroyed east pediment of the Parthenon, which depicted the birth of Athena, dates back 40 years.
  • In 1986, he scaled ancient Greece’s most famous temple at night by rope to examine the base of the east pediment under special lamps that function only without ambient light, hoping to find traces left by 39 lost sculpted figures over the main gate.
  • “Nothing came of that,” states Brinkmann, who is now the head of antiquities at the Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection in Frankfurt—except, he adds, rumours about ghosts on the Acropolis that flew around Athens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vinzenz Brinkmann’s quest to solve the mysteries of the destroyed east pediment of the Parthenon, which depicted the birth of Athena, dates back 40 years.

In 1986, he scaled ancient Greece’s most famous temple at night by rope to examine the base of the east pediment under special lamps that function only without ambient light, hoping to find traces left by 39 lost sculpted figures over the main gate.

“Nothing came of that,” states Brinkmann, who is now the head of antiquities at the Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection in Frankfurt—except, he adds, rumours about ghosts on the Acropolis that flew around Athens.

But now, Brinkmann states his team has solved a riddle akin to “putting together a jigsaw puzzle without having all the pieces”. The results of decades of research will go on show in an exhibition, Athena, the Stage is Yours: the Parthenon Puzzle, opening at the Liebieghaus on 18 November.

Long a flashpoint in Greek-British relations, the politics of the Parthenon surfaced in the run-up to the opening. The exhibition was to include marble fragments from both the British Museum in London and the Acropolis Museum in Athens. But, as The Art Newspaper reported last month, the Greek government withdrew its loan of nine fragments: according to Greek media reports, the request was rejected by Greece’s Central Archaeological Council on the grounds that they would be shown alongside British Museum pieces removed from the Acropolis by Lord Elgin. The Greek ministry of culture’s press office did not respond to emailed requests for comment and confirmation.

It has been revealed that greece has for decades demanded the return of the Parthenon Marbles taken by Elgin, which have been housed in the British Museum since 1817. The Liebieghaus has, however, secured a rare loan of two fragments from the British Museum. After the Greek government’s withdrawal, a British Museum spokesperson confirmed that the museum “will still be loaning”.

Industry observers note that “The cancellation of the loans from Greece does not detract from the exhibition’s concept, or its scholarly significance,” declares Elisabeth Pallentin, a spokesperson for the Liebieghaus. “The exhibition is based primarily on newly introduced findings resulting from many years of research at the Liebieghaus.”.

Recent findings suggest that the east pediment is probably “the most famous image of antiquity”, Brinkmann says, with the centre of the sculpted ensemble composed of 3.5m-tall figures. The pediment was destroyed at some point between the fifth century AD and 1670—it is not known when or why, though there are plenty of theories—and 80% of it is still missing.

Sources indicate that the rest is in fragments in museums around the world. Until now, no one had succeeded in fully reconstructing the central figures, Brinkmann says. “In the last 200 years, there have been a lot of proposals, but we saw that there were always gaps.”.

A reconstruction of the figures in the east pediment of the Parthenon (detail).

Vinzenz Brinkmann and Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, 2026. Liebieghaus Skulpturensammlung, Frankfurt am Main.

It has been revealed that the most serious work on the east pediment had been undertaken more than a century ago by a British Museum curator, Arthur Hamilton Smith, Brinkmann says. Smith partially recreated the east pediment using plaster casts from the British Museum and cooperated with colleagues in Athens to obtain more casts; his reconstruction went on display in the museum in 1908.

It has been revealed that “He did a fantastic job in preparing the way,” Brinkmann states. “That was our basis.”.

Industry observers note that although the Liebieghaus team recreated these fragments using scans and a 3D printer, the majority of the pediment was still missing. A breakthrough came when the team began investigating reliefs from the lids of Roman sarcophagi, which proved the key to unlocking the mystery.

“It was really a chance discovery,” Brinkmann states. “During a visit to the Hermitage in St Petersburg in 2014, we noticed a figural relief on the lid of a sarcophagus that was clearly closely related to the composition of the east pediment. It refers to the few surviving figures from the corners of the pediment, such as Helios and Selene with their chariots, but also to figures that have repeatedly been proposed as having belonged to the east pediment, such as the Horae/Moirai.”.

They discovered nine sarcophagi in total with relevant reliefs. Most were in the Vatican Museums and elsewhere in Rome. “They had been overlooked,” Brinkmann says. “But the Romans copied everything the Greeks did.”.

Jaques Carrey, drawing of the east pediment (left-hand side), Temple of Minerva, Athens (1674).

Bibliothèque nationale de France, ref.: FOL-FC-3.

None of these reliefs showed the entire east pediment ensemble; each depicted a different subset of the 39 figures. But with the aid of computer technology, the team established that the remaining fragments of the east pediment and the depictions on the reliefs were a 100% match.

Industry observers note that the team’s research has yielded some surprises. It was not previously known, for instance, that the Dioscuri, the twin horsemen known as Castor and Pollux to the Romans, were portrayed on the pediment. The figures served as models for the giant figures on the Quirinale in Rome, which are almost identical and date from antiquity, Brinkmann claims. The twins are portrayed standing next to their bucking horses with anxious expressions, straining at the reins in an effort to control them.

In a recent development, this portrayal of the Dioscuri makes sense only in the context of the birth of the goddess, Brinkmann says. In mythology, Athena burst forth from her father Zeus’s forehead after he had swallowed her mother. Her birth is described in the Homeric hymns as causing Mount Olympus to shake, the earth to shriek, and the sea to swell and rage.

Industry observers note that “The Dioscuri are heroic horsemen in mythology,” Brinkmann states. “They don’t lose control of their horses. But the birth of Athena was a primordial cosmic event that unleashed a natural disaster. What we see are the consequences.” Other figures in the recreated ensemble are also responding to the cataclysm: Hermes, for instance, is depicted holding onto his hat.

Brinkmann is known internationally for his research into polychromy in ancient Greek and Roman sculpture. An exhibition he curated, Gods in Color—Painted Sculpture of Classical Antiquity, has travelled the world, having been shown in several US locations, Athens, Oxford, Istanbul, the Vatican Museums and elsewhere.

It is possible that the fresh Liebieghaus exhibition will travel too, Brinkmann notes. But not, it seems, with marbles from the Athens collections, with recent developments giving little room to hope that a lasting settlement between Greece and the British Museum is on the horizon.

• Athena, the Stage is Yours, Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection, Frankfurt, 18 November-25 July 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wolff Olins builds the Hyundai Card brand identity on Architect of Change: a fixed core, and a generative color system for every card.
  • The Purple, one of the upcoming card faces, fills its surface with a dotted halftone field in deep violet, and the name sits small in a light grotesque at the top left, next to the chip.
  • A fixed core never moves: the logo sits in the same place, in the same open bracket frame, carried by the same typeface on every card.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wolff Olins builds the Hyundai Card brand identity on Architect of Change: a fixed core, and a generative color system for every card.

The card is the poster here. The Purple, one of the upcoming card faces, fills its surface with a dotted halftone field in deep violet, and the name sits small in a light grotesque at the top left, next to the chip. The same violet bleeds into a painted field behind the card, so object and world share one color. Wolff Olins spent time in Seoul before drawing anything, talking with customers and young Koreans. More than eight in ten South Koreans in their twenties still live with their parents, so people define themselves through taste and through what they choose to carry. A card notes something about who you are and who you intend to become, and that became the design problem.

The system runs on a simple split. A fixed core never moves: the logo sits in the same place, in the same open bracket frame, carried by the same typeface on every card. Around that core, each card gets its own world. The entry cards, M, X and Z, use a generative system of bright color and repetition, so no two faces repeat the same pattern. A type specimen sheet sets the grotesque in full, and the card specification drawing marks the 1.58 ratio every face must hold.

Scale does the talking in the applications. The wordmark stays small and bracketed while a single figure, 93 percent, fills a whole green panel, and the card faces run at poster size on street walls. The card ratio repeats across posters, totes and packaging, so the system reads as one object cut to different sizes.

According to recent reports, the physical pieces carry the same discipline. Modular packaging holds the whole range together: a grey box with a debossed Hyundai Card mark and a red peel tab, each card sealed in a protective layer that peels back to reveal its character. The dotted halftone on the Purple card reads as texture before it reads as pattern. The tote bag carries the bracketed wordmark on green, with a black band at the base.

Recent findings suggest that color is the flex in the system. Violet owns the Purple card, acid green owns the commercial card and the big figures, and black and grey hold everything together. The butterfly image reveals what the generative color does when it leaves the card: the same violet, painted loose across a wing, with the pattern breaking into dots. Every card keeps the same bones and gets a different skin.

See more from Wolff Olins on their site.

  • Located in Manhattan’s SoHo neighbourhood, the flagship store for Ferrari’s fashion label is in a long, narrow building at the corner of Prince Street and Mercer Street and spreads across two levels.
  • Berlin-based Gonzalez Haase AAS clad the building in brushed metal, with curved window mullions covering floor-to-ceiling glass along its length.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy Ferrari Style.

Architecture studios Gonzalez Haase AAS and Formafantasma have worked with Ferrari Style creative director Rocco Iannone on the brand’s first permanent store in Newly introduced York, clad in a metallic facade.

Located in Manhattan’s SoHo neighbourhood, the flagship store for Ferrari’s fashion label is in a long, narrow building at the corner of Prince Street and Mercer Street and spreads across two levels.

Berlin-based Gonzalez Haase AAS clad the building in brushed metal, with curved window mullions covering floor-to-ceiling glass along its length.

It has been revealed that under Iannone, the team referenced the Ferrari Officina concept, a central theme of the brand that seeks to connect fashion and automotive. It considers “the workshop as a junction at which artistic instinct, scientific rigour, craftsmanship and mechanical precision converge,” according to the team.

“The Officina is the place where intuition is given form through discipline, and where the human touch works in harmony with mechanical precision,” said Iannone.

The opening follows another Ferrari Style store opened earlier this year in London, designed by the same team, and both stores share pops of red, warm beige finishes, and steel accents.

However, the New York space was designed to fit in with the city. The team said the New York location reflects the “form, scale and material character of SoHo”.

“For New York, we wanted to translate this spirit into a space in which architecture, fashion and object design each retain their own identity while contributing to a single Ferrari language,” said the team.

“Every material and detail has been chosen to express this balance between art and science, creating an environment that is open, evolving and in direct dialogue with the energy of SoHo.”.

Men’s ready-to-wear is located on the first floor, with objects displayed on units designed by Formafantasma.

The space is bordered by a deep red curtain and large rectangular ceiling lights.

A staircase to the left side of the store leads to the “more intimate” second level, containing women’s ready-to-wear, footwear and accessories collections.

It also contains the store’s atelier, the second worldwide apart from the London location.

Wrapped in leather curtains, the space provides a private setting for personalisations and alterations. A table containing samples of textiles and hardware sits at the centre.

Ferrari Style, the brand’s luxury fashion line founded in 2021, has other US locations in New Jersey, Miami, and Las Vegas.

Ferrari recently unveiled a laptop collaboration with HP, as well as its first electric vehicle earlier this year.

Photography courtesy Ferrari Style.

Latest Update: South London Gallery director Margot Heller to leave role after 25 years

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Margot Heller, the director of the South London Gallery, will step down from her position in May 2027 after more than 25 years.
  • Heller, who joined SLG in 2001, plans to become an independent curator and adviser.
  • “After 25 years at the helm, I feel it’s time for latest adventures in my career,” Heller said in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Margot Heller, the director of the South London Gallery, will step down from her position in May 2027 after more than 25 years. Over this time the institution’s physical footprint has more than tripled and visitor numbers increased tenfold, according to a gallery statement.

Heller, who joined SLG in 2001, plans to become an independent curator and adviser. She will retain a connection with the gallery, curating the Dutch artist’s Mark Manders’s first solo exhibition at a London institution, opening at SLG on 23 September 2027.

“After 25 years at the helm, I feel it’s time for latest adventures in my career,” Heller said in a statement.

Industry observers note that “From the day I took up the role, I saw an opportunity to build an institution that could be internationally acclaimed for its contemporary art programme, and deeply embedded in its local community. I have stayed true to that vision ever since.”.

Serge Ramin, the chair of the gallery’s trustees, described Heller as “a visionary curator and cultural leader”, adding: “She leaves a museum that is artistically ambitious, rooted in its community and physically transformed.”.

Heller’s tenure encompassed two major building projects with 6a architects: the conversion of a neighbouring house and construction of an education studio in 2010, followed by the opening of the former Peckham Road Fire Station in 2018.

According to recent reports, the fire station was donated in 2014 by the artist Raqib Shaw, whose identity was initially withheld. Its conversion cost £4m. Heller told The Art Newspaper in 2018 that the gallery had not been actively seeking to expand when the building was offered.

A garden designed by Gabriel Orozco opened in 2016, while Art Block, the gallery’s free space for children and young people on the neighbouring Sceaux Gardens estate, opened at its current site in 2017.

The artist and SLG trustee Alvaro Barrington mentioned: “In Margot’s time at the South London Gallery she has created pivotal moments in many artists’ careers, including my own.”.

He added: “Her commissioning of the Orozco Garden should be considered one of the most notable architectural interventions in the UK.”.

In a recent development, exhibitions Heller has worked on during her tenure include solo presentations by Steve McQueen, Rashid Johnson, Oscar Murillo, Michael Armitage and Christina Quarles. The gallery was a joint winner of Art Fund’s Museum of the Year award in 2020.

Before joining the SLG, Heller worked at Southampton City Art Gallery, becoming its director, and as director of exhibitions at Anthony d’Offay Gallery. She was appointed OBE (Officer of the Order of the British Empire) in 2014.

The gallery became an independent charity in 2003, having previously been managed by Southwark Council.

Joy Gregory, an artist and SLG trustee, noted of Heller in a statement: “As a local resident and artist, I am enormously grateful for the extraordinary legacy she leaves behind and excited to see what she does next.”.

Latest Update: Ocean liner sunk in Florida to become "world's largest artificial reef"

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (539 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography courtesy of Destin-Fort Walton Beach.
  • On Wednesday, the ocean liner SS United States was sunk 180 feet underwater to become an artificial reef off the coast of Florida.
  • The sinking took approximately eight hours, and dozens of onlookers and officials looked on as the ship underwent a controlled deployment, or scuttling, to the bottom of the ocean.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy of Destin-Fort Walton Beach.

On Wednesday, the ocean liner SS United States was sunk 180 feet underwater to become an artificial reef off the coast of Florida.

The sinking took approximately eight hours, and dozens of onlookers and officials looked on as the ship underwent a controlled deployment, or scuttling, to the bottom of the ocean.

The ship will join a long stretch of artificial reefs, including 580 other decommissioned vessels and structures, that line the ocean floor off the coast Destin-Fort Walton Beach, Florida.

“A newly introduced chapter has begun in Destin-Fort Walton Beach, Florida, where the legendary SS United States, once the fastest ocean liner in the world, has completed her final voyage to become the World’s Largest Artificial Reef,” remarked a release from the government of Destin-Fort Walton Beach.

The site serves as a tourist and dive destination for SCUBA divers both new and seasoned, as the underwater structures are meant to provide infrastructure for marine life.

“Beyond its appeal as a dive destination, the SS United States will serve an notable environmental purpose,” noted the team.

“Her massive structure will provide new habitat for marine life, supporting the growth of an underwater ecosystem that includes inhabitants such as sea turtles, grouper, snapper and marlin.”.

In preparation for its scuttling, the ship underwent a years-long remediation process, where it was stripped of toxic materials, such as green neotex exterior floor covering and paint.

Elements such as the ventilation system, wiring and the propeller were also removed, with the latter stored for a land-based museum that will accompany the dive site.

“To see a project of this magnitude become a reality is an incredible moment for our team and for the future of marine conservation,” said Destin-Fort Walton Beach natural resources chief Alex Fogg.

“This is so much more than creating a upcoming dive destination. It’s an opportunity to advance marine science on a scale we’ve never experienced before. The sheer scale of the SS United States presents a rare opportunity to study how an artificial reef of this size transforms over time.”.

In a recent development, the project has been years in the making. The ship, designed by naval architect William Francis Gibb and known for its speed, served as a passenger vessel between 1952 and 1969.

It was decommissioned in 1969, and eventually bought to a Philadelphia harbour in the 1990s, where it sat inactive for decades as various owners bought and then sold the vessel in failed attempts to restore it and make it profitable.

In 2009, the non-profit SS United States Conservancy purchased and began stewarding the ship.

In 2024, due to rent complications, the ship could no longer stay berthed at its Philadelphia pier, and the SS United States Conservancy sold it to Okaloosa County, Florida, for $1 million.

As of today, it stands upright in its intended position, and its uppermost deck is accessible to divers, who can “now enjoy the site”.

Other artificial reefs around the world include the Reefline project in Miami, which is set to feature underwater sculpture designed by OMA and a LEGO-inspired modular system designed by Alex Goad, intended to restore damaged coral reefs.

Photography courtesy of Destin-Fort Walton Beach.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

North Korean state media has published a series of propaganda photos starring supreme leader Kim Jong Un and his heir apparent daughter.

The rare images published by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) have caused an online sensation thanks to Kim Jong Un’s outrageous pose: smoking a cigarette while sitting on a throne-like chair at a ski resort.

Kim watched as his daughter Ju Ae (although her name has never been officially confirmed) hit the slopes, smiling as she carved the snow.

The photos were taken by KCNA over the weekend, capturing Kim Jong Un and his daughter visiting Samjiyon, a tourist town that’s being built close to the Chinese border. Under construction are Samjiyon airport, a tourist railway line, and a ski resort.

According to KCNA, Kim pronounced the resort’s hotels, lodges​, and housing “flawless and worthy of top marks.”.

That his daughter, Ju Ae, features prominently in the photos is telling. South Korean intelligence believes she has been selected as his heir. She is thought to be 13 years old and still in training to take over the Kim dynasty that has ruled North Korea with an iron fist for almost 80 years. She would be the fourth Kim and the first female if she were to succeed her father.

North Korean state media does not publish photos accidentally, and the fact that Ju Ae has been photographed standing shoulder to shoulder with her father carries symbolic weight.

The internet lapped up the North Korean propaganda photos, saying that despotic Kim has “aura.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The UK government has temporarily blocked two 16th-century volumes of Mughal calligraphy from being taken out of the country permanently.

The export bar, which allows time for a UK gallery or institution to acquire the calligraphy works, will initially expire on 15 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £900,000, followed by a second deferral period of four months.

“By keeping the volumes in the country, it is hoped researchers can study how the construction of such calligraphic collections has evolved. Given so few works of this kind survive intact, its preservation makes it especially valuable,” states a statement from the UK Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS). The volumes were kept in a private collection from the 1980s until 2020 when they were sold at Sotheby’s London for £620,000 (before fees) to a specialist dealer in London.

In a recent development, the calligraphic works, thought to be over 400 years old, are spread across 29 leaves and feature gold ornamentation of plant and animal motifs. The two volumes derive from an imperial album created around 1595-1605.

According to the DCMS statement, the original album was prepared for Mughal Emperor Akbar or his son Prince Salim at the royal workshop either in Lahore or Agra. Muhammad Hussain Kashmiri and Abd al-Rahim al-Haravi are among the calligraphers featured.

The Black Prince marble bust by Michael Rysbrack (around 1735).

Courtesy Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport.

In a recent development, meanwhile another export bar has been placed on a marble bust of the 14th-century prince Edward of Woodstock, the son of King Edward III of England and popularly known as the Black Prince. Created around 1735, the sculpture was made by the Flemish sculptor, Michael Rysbrack.

This export bar will initially expire on 5 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £496,044 plus VAT, followed by a second deferral period of four months.

Fiona Twycross, the heritage minister, indicates in a statement: “For nearly three hundred years [the sculpture] has shaped how we tell the story of our medieval history and I hope that in a public gallery in the UK it can tell that story much more powerfully for many more years to come.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Capture One and Hasselblad have jointly revealed that real-time, wired tethered shooting for the X2D II 100C is now supported in Capture One with the latest versions of the camera’s firmware and Capture One software.

Tethered shooting support was revealed as in the works back in July when Hasselblad first revealed its partnership with Capture One.

According to recent reports, “There is a well-documented history between Hasselblad and Phase One, and we’re not here to dwell on it. Capture One has operated as an independent company since 2020, and what matters to us is serving photographers,” Capture One’s CEO Rafael Orta told PetaPixel last summer. “And they have asked us for this for years — on forums, in feature requests, in conversations. That’s why we’ve been working for a while with the Hasselblad team to deliver their shooters a native Capture One workflow.”.

Now, not only can Hasselblad photographers edit their X2D II RAW files inside of Capture One, the full studio workflow is supported through tethering. Each image will appear on screen at full resolution at nearly the same moment it is captured when connected with a USB tethering cable. Hasselblad notes that photographers can check focus and exposure while the set is still live and nobody has moved.

“[That] means no waiting around or breaking the flow. The full Capture One toolset is available from the first shot, so the grades and masks photographers apply to the first frame carry over to all subsequent shots,” Hasselblad says.

In a recent development, studio photographers don’t need any convincing as to the value of tethering, but those who are less familiar might not know that the capability is hugely important for commercial sets where clients are on hand. It’s far easier to set clients at a digital tech workstation watching a monitor as results come in rather than hovering over a photographer’s shoulder trying to get a look at the rear LCD.

“This means creative direction and collaboration happen in real time, turning every session into a truly collaborative shoot,” the two companies add.

“We are always listening to our photographers, and tethering support for Hasselblad cameras was one of the top requests when our collaboration with Capture One was revealed earlier this year,” Bronius Rudnickas, Global Marketing Manager at Hasselblad, says. “We are delighted that this workflow option is now available, giving Hasselblad photographers and creatives worldwide greater flexibility in their creative journeys.”.

Wired tethering for the Hasselblad X2D II 100C is available starting today in Capture One 16.9.1 for desktop and Mobile 4.3.0, requiring X2D II 100C firmware version 1.4.15.7.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Igor Nora builds the Parniera brand identity from silk and sculpted gold, with a bespoke typeface and a silk moth mark in pale yellow.

Industry observers note that the idea is a collision the project calls Sculpted Duality. On one side, fine silk in fluid motion, pale yellow, soft and light. On the other, solid sculpted gold forms with architectural weight. The identity holds both at once: garments described as vulnerability and armor, built for a woman who commands the room with quiet power. Nothing shouts. The yellow field does the talking, and the black line work sits on it with total control.

The wordmark is a bespoke typeface drawn for the house. Thin, delicate strokes carry the lightness, while high contrast serifs give the letters their structure. The detail that holds it together is the ligatures: internal connective strokes, clearest in the N, I, E and R, link the characters the way woven silk holds a thread, so the name reads as one continuous piece. A construction frame reveals the letters PA on black, with guide bars and notes on the straight serifs and the joins between letters.

The moth mark works the same way. It is built from four overlapping geometric forms, a line drawing of the Bombyx mori silk moth, the living link between the Persian name Parnia, a canvas of fine silk, and the sculpted gold the house stands for.

It has been revealed that the system stays physical wherever it lands. The moth mark sits alone on a pale yellow tile, then repeats as a woven petal pattern in yellow, gold and tan. The brand book opens in a black ring binder: a yellow page carries the wordmark embossed into the paper, facing a white page headed "Essence of allure." The same yellow carries the shopping bag, the wordmark pressed into the paper along the bottom edge, with black ribbon handles.

At street level the system scales up without changing its voice. A tall yellow banner hangs on a red brick building beside a panel with the moth mark, and the closing collage pulls the whole world together: moth tile, beaded gown detail, patterned envelope, shopping bag, the wordmark on yellow, and the line "Presence without the noise." It is a quiet luxury, stated once and left alone.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NBA superstar LeBron James has sued the makers of an AI sports-betting app for allegedly using AI-generated images of him in its marketing.

On Tuesday, James filed a lawsuit in the Southern District of New York against the founders of Bron, an AI-powered sports-betting app. The lawsuit focuses on a video ad released by the Bron app’s founders earlier this month. It shows an AI-generated version of James using the Bron app to bet on basketball games from a locker room.

According to the complaint, the ad depicts James wearing a basketball jersey bearing his nickname and the iconic number 23. It also reproduces his tattoos and a simulated version of his voice. The video shows the AI-generated figure scrolling through NBA betting options on the app.

“The ad catapulted the Bron app from obscurity to controversy, with the ad gaining a million views within a day — exactly as defendants intended,” James argues in the civil complaint, according to a report by Courthouse News Service.

It has been revealed that the complaint also notes the AI-generated image of the basketball star “falsely communicates that Mr. James wagers, or considers wagering, on NBA games and NBA player ​performance—conduct that NBA rules prohibit.”.

James argues that the depiction of him sitting in a locker room and betting on basketball could also harm his reputation.

“This is at odds with Mr. James’s well-known and highly televised routine of being on time for games and being one of the first people out on the court,” he argues.

James also claims that the app’s name was chosen to attract attention by exploiting his well-known “Bron” nickname. He accuses PlayVision, the company that operates the app, and its co-founders, Anish Gupta and Marc Zoghby, of deliberately using the name to mislead consumers into thinking he endorsed or was affiliated with the product.

Recent findings suggest that james’s lawyers sent the manufacturer a cease-and-desist letter on November 5. Following the letter, the startup removed the ad from X (the platform formerly known as Twitter) and Instagram and stated it was working to change the app’s name, according to the complaint. However, the lawsuit alleges that the video remained available through third-party reposts and that the company had not changed the app’s name by the time the lawsuit was filed.

LeBron’s lawsuit comes after Norwegian soccer player Erling Haaland sued an airline last month over a social media post that featured an edited image referencing his distinctive hairstyle during the 2026 World Cup.

A photographer had an incredible encounter with a famous grizzly bear known as “The Boss” in Banff, Canada.

According to recent reports, jason Leo Bantle was in Banff National Park when he came across fresh bear tracks in the snow. Knowing the substantial bruin must be in the area, Bantle came back on November 6 and spotted The Boss foraging along the railway tracks that run through the park.

“Known for grains being dropped from railcars or other animals being hit, The Boss has learned that when food is not plentiful in the backcountry, the tracks may offer some subsistence,” Bantle tells PetaPixel.

Bantle is aware of the risks of approaching a grizzly in the wild, so he waited at a great distance, observing the bear through an 840mm telephoto lens and binoculars.

Industry observers note that the Fresh York Times ran an article over the weekend about The Boss. It revealed that he is categorized as “habituated” by the park’s management, which means he is not bothered by people so long as he is left alone.

Sources indicate that “The biggest thing is his gentleness and his respect towards the people,” Paul Klra, a gas station owner and photographer, told The Times. “He has never done any harm to anyone.”.

In a recent development, while The Boss has never done any harm to humans, he certainly has done harm to other bears. His biggest rival in the area is a bear called Split Lip; The Boss gave him that lip.

It has been revealed that he’s also survived being struck by a train and has been known to kill and eat black bears. However, a park ecologist tells The Times that 90% of The Boss’s diet is made up of berries, roots, and other plants.

“As a professional photographer, you are focused on your craft and capturing an image that is the essence of the animal and their environment, so you do lose yourself in the moment,” Bantle indicates of photographing The Boss.

According to recent reports, “I always reflect back on moments like this with The Boss; he is a living legend! The one image of him as he lumbered toward me with light snow falling was just magnificent: the grandeur of this bear, an apex predator, yet the gentleness of his quiet presence — no wind and a light snowfall, it was humbling to be in his presence.”.

Industry observers note that the Boss is thought to be 28 years old, advanced for a bear. He has become internationally famous, and it makes the news when he comes out of hibernation.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists captured extraordinary footage of two gorillas climbing on each other’s backs and forming a “living ladder” to reach a high branch on a tree that was out of reach.
  • The pair of female western lowland gorillas were filmed displaying what researchers describe as rare behavior in their species: one positioned herself to provide a stable platform while the other climbed onto her back to reach vegetation they could not access individually.
  • Sources indicate that researchers from Tel Aviv University documented the behavior at the Ramat Gan Safari in Israel, recording three separate instances of spontaneous cooperation between the adult gorillas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists captured extraordinary footage of two gorillas climbing on each other’s backs and forming a “living ladder” to reach a high branch on a tree that was out of reach.

The pair of female western lowland gorillas were filmed displaying what researchers describe as rare behavior in their species: one positioned herself to provide a stable platform while the other climbed onto her back to reach vegetation they could not access individually.

Sources indicate that researchers from Tel Aviv University documented the behavior at the Ramat Gan Safari in Israel, recording three separate instances of spontaneous cooperation between the adult gorillas. According to a study published in the journal Primates, the events took place in 2021, 2024, and 2025 and involved the same two half-sisters, Amelia and Lisha.

According to recent reports, in each instance, the gorillas performed the same roles. Lisha provided a stable platform, while Amelia climbed onto her back to reach nearby branches. Neither animal had been trained to perform the behavior.

The most extensively documented event occurred in September 2024, when keepers noticed the two females peacefully eating bark and leaves from a large branch that had previously been beyond their reach. To find out how they had accessed the food, staff reviewed security camera footage.

According to recent reports, the recordings revealed a coordinated series of actions. Amelia first walked over and climbed onto a rock beneath a Peltophorum dubium tree. Lisha then joined her, standing firmly on all fours on the rock. Amelia climbed onto Lisha’s back, stood upright, and stretched upward to grasp and break off a branch approximately 15 feet above the ground.

The combination of the rock, Lisha’s stable position, and Amelia’s additional height allowed her to reach the branch. An electric barrier around the tree trunk prevented the gorillas from climbing it directly.

Michael Levitzky, who initiated and led the study, says the footage indicates genuine cooperation, with Leisha independently choosing to help Amelia achieve their shared goal rather than simply being used as a tool.

It has been revealed that “When I first watched the footage, it was clear to me that this was something extraordinary. What I find fascinating is that Leisha did more than simply serve as a ‘step’ for Amelia,” Levitzky says in a statement. “She appeared to participate actively and willingly in solving the problem, approaching on her own initiative and positioning herself in exactly the right place, without Amelia physically guiding her. This is the difference between using another individual as a tool and true cooperation, in which both individuals work together toward the same goal.

Levitzky notes that gorillas may be more socially and cognitively intelligent than previously thought, and that further research could reveal more about how they cooperate and what this tells us about the origins of cooperation in humans.

Industry observers note that “For years, gorillas were considered less cognitively sophisticated than other great apes,” Levitzky explains. “As more observations like these accumulate, we will be able to deepen and refine our understanding of their social and cognitive abilities. Future studies involving systematic documentation and audio recordings could help us decipher how they coordinate with one another, and perhaps also teach us something about the roots of cooperation in our own species.”.

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Latest bi-national art initiative reframes stereotypes about Mexico-US border

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1288 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Can the “open wound” of the Mexico-US border be healed?
  • Juárez has long been associated with sensational narratives of violence.
  • It has been revealed that though seemingly worlds apart today, Ciudad Juárez and El Paso were one city until the Rio Grande river was established as the border between Mexico and the US in 1848.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Can the “open wound” of the Mexico-US border be healed? Sutura, a newly introduced bi-national art programme in Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, and El Paso, Texas (18 November-22 November), looks beyond stereotypes of violence surrounding the Mexico-US border and explores how art might help mend the region’s many wounds, even imperfectly or temporarily. Sutura (Spanish for “suture”) brings together more than 100 artists across 20 venues, including the El Paso Museum of Art (EPMA), the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts and the Museo de Arte de Ciudad Juárez (MACJ), alongside independent projects and pop-up exhibitions.

Juárez has long been associated with sensational narratives of violence. Persistent migration issues, heightened by stricter border controls and alarming deportation measures, feminicides, the drug war and hyper-surveillance have shaped the local context. These aspects have permeated cultural production. “Endless works have explored this territory as a symbol and symptom of an apocalyptic future,” writes Willivaldo Delgadillo in his book-length essay Fabular Juárez (2020).

It has been revealed that though seemingly worlds apart today, Ciudad Juárez and El Paso were one city until the Rio Grande river was established as the border between Mexico and the US in 1848. Despite tensions between their respective countries, the two cities are still connected by education, jobs and transit.

“On each side of the border, nuanced and contrasting fears and ideologies coexist, but there is also community,” Edgar Picazo Merino, Sutura’s founder and lead organiser, tells The Art Newspaper. “For all of us who live here, the border is a personal, lived experience.” Picazo founded the independent initiative Azul Arena in 2019 to support the Juárez-El Paso art scene; it established a permanent space in Juárez in 2022.

In a recent development, central to thinking about the border in the context of Sutura and more broadly is Chicana writer Gloria Anzaldúa’s 1987 metaphor of the border as an “open wound”. “The Third World grates against the first and bleeds,” Anzaldúa wrote. “And before a scab forms, it haemorrhages again, the lifeblood of two worlds merging to form a third country—a border culture.” The “open wound” concept has become commonplace in border literature, Picazo states, while Sutura seeks to deconstruct it: “If the border is a wound, how can the arts suture its many wounds, while opening places of reflection and interaction?”.

Detail of Justin Favela's Mantecore (White Tiger) (2017), featured in Qué tanto es tantito, a group show on view at San Luis Contemporáneo, Ciudad Juárez Courtesy Haydee Alonso.

Sutura builds on binational initiatives like Insite, which emerged in 1992 at the San Diego-Tijuana border and initially featured site-specific installations before changing formats. It also draws on regional ties. The Juárez-El Paso Border Biennial, debuted in 2008 by the EPMA and MACJ, is at the moment in its eighth edition, Imagining the Border (until 2 May 2027). Co-curated by the Juárez-based curators Adriana Miramontes Olivas and Alejandro Morales, it features more than 80 works by artists based within 300 miles of El Paso and Juárez.

“A border that is always there, one that weighs heavily on our communities, rarely lets us imagine it,” Morales claims. “This edition opens that space, offering a plural and rigorous portrait of it as living territory.”.

It has been revealed that the Border Biennial has strived to shift perceptions. “The biennial has national relevance, moving beyond portrayals of the border as perpetually on fire, highlighting its creative richness and cultural legacies,” states Edward Hayes Jr, the director of the EPMA, adding that the project requires overcoming diplomatic and logistical challenges. “We aim for the biennial to be a structural project for both institutions,” says Christian Diego Diego, MACJ’s director. Diego adds that over its past and current editions, the Border Biennial has featured more than 400 works by around 270 artists, “reflecting the border’s ambivalence and multiple stories”. Sutura’s programme includes visits to the biennial, reflecting dialogue with the artists, curators and venues.

Industry observers note that sutura also grew from asking how a Juárez-El Paso art week might unfold. Border initiatives are gaining visibility. The fair Material, through its two-year Projects programme, has supported Azul Arena and the Juárez curatorial duo Un Dique with mentorship and free participation in its Mexico City and Guadalajara fairs. Un Dique joins Sutura by curating theexhibition Border Kaijus on border hypervigilance. Two other border cities have recently created art weeks amid growing efforts to decentralise a national scene largely centred on Mexico City: Tijuana held its second art week in July; Mexicali held its first in April.

In a recent development, “There is a growing scene among border Mexican cities with spaces and initiatives interacting,” notes Andres Payan Estrada, the director and chief curator of the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts and Sutura’s artistic strategy director. Still, he adds, Sutura is not an art week: “It is a non-commercial collaborative initiative with a strong community component.”.

Installation view of the group show Costuras Territoriales at the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts at the University of Texas, El Paso Courtesy of the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts at the University of Texas, El Paso.

Recent findings suggest that in El Paso, institutional participation is strong. During Sutura, the Rubin Center is showing Costuras Territoriales (until 12 December), curated by Payan and featuring textile-inspired works by five women artists connected to the border, including Teresa Margolles, Tania Candiani and Juárez-based Olga Guerra. “The way in which artists explore the border has sometimes become a cliché,” Guerra says. “I intend to reflect relationality through a more poetic approach, incorporating locally found organic materials and fibres, along with reused materials.”.

According to recent reports, independent initiatives are vital in Juárez, where conventional galleries are non-existent. Picazo’s Azul Arena, a pillar of the city’s scene, will present the exhibition En la línea, exploring the line as a metaphor for the border. The Juárez-based artist Haydee Alonso, co-founder of San Luis Contemporáneo, will curate the exhibition ¿Qué tanto es tantito? there and present a performance at Azul Arena. “My work analyses transborder relations through the body and objects, opening spaces within the complexities of living here,” claims Alonso, who crosses the border daily to teach at the University of Texas at El Paso. Both projects have received support from the Mellon Foundation, which Alonso and Picazo consider crucial to local initiatives. In El Paso, where independent spaces are relatively scarce, The Falstaff, a community-centred hybrid art space, will host exhibitions and concerts.

Installation view ofthe group exhibiton Qué tanto es tantito, group show on view at San Luis Contemporáneo, Ciudad Juárez Courtesy Haydee Alonso.

Sutura also supports the local scene by showcasing six El Paso and Juárez projects selected through an open call, with each project receiving $3,000 for production costs. The photography exhibition Relatos de la Frontera: Cuerpo y Espacio explores border perspectives through the body and space Another show, Tierra Suelta, presents works inspired by children of migrant families that settled in Juárez for reasons other than the “American dream”, integrating a community activation into the programme. These projects foreground local perspectives in a region often depicted by outsiders, alongside established artists—primarily Mexican and Mexican American—whose work reflects on the border.

Picazo acknowledges the complexities of a bi-national event: not everyone can cross both ways because of visa restrictions and other challenges. “The programme has parallel activities so you can experience Sutura even from one side of the border,” he notes.

It has been revealed that sutura speaks more of resilience than crisis, more of possibility than scarcity.“Historically, the border is explained one-dimensionally, yet a myriad of dynamics co-exist here,” Picazo claims. “Sutura exists as a relational art encounter.”.

  • The feature is called Content Protection, and it allows eligible creators to monitor copies of their videos across Instagram and Facebook and decide how to respond when a match is detected.
  • Once enrolled, creators will receive alerts when Instagram identifies a visual match of one of their original videos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Instagram is rolling out a upcoming tool designed to help creators identify and manage unauthorized copies of their videos, as the platform responds to growing concerns about content theft and the use of AI to reproduce original work.

The feature is called Content Protection, and it allows eligible creators to monitor copies of their videos across Instagram and Facebook and decide how to respond when a match is detected. Meta previously introduced a similar tool on Facebook and is now bringing the feature to Instagram.

Once enrolled, creators will receive alerts when Instagram identifies a visual match of one of their original videos. They can then choose to monitor the copied video’s performance, hide it from Instagram and Facebook, add an attribution link directing viewers to the original video, or release their claim and allow the content to remain on the platform.

Sources indicate that techCrunch reports that creators who enroll will have newly introduced original videos automatically protected. They can also manually select eligible videos published before enrolling. Accounts that have permission to use a creator’s work, such as a second profile or a brand account, can be added to an allow list to prevent their content from being flagged.

Recent findings suggest that instagram is also expanding its detection capabilities to address AI-generated content. The platform will begin testing a feature that identifies videos using audio from a creator’s original work, including spoken words, even when the original visuals have been replaced with AI-generated imagery.

The firm notes it is also exploring ways to limit the reach of accounts and content that repeatedly use AI tools to repurpose other creators’ work.

The rollout comes as creators face increasing difficulties protecting their material from AI-generated copies. Videos featuring altered faces, fictional performers, and recreated comedy routines have become a growing concern, particularly for creators whose work is reused without attribution.

Comedian Sarah Purdum tells Mashable she discovered her material had been repurposed by an AI account.

“It seems to be that female comedians’ work is being stolen and repurposed for sexy AI models,” she indicates. “I feel annoyed that my work is being taken for the purpose of drawing in men.”.

Other design news included Swedish designer Gustaf Westman’s unveiling of his full collection for media manufacturer Disney, including a bookstand shaped like Donald Duck and a mirror that resembles Pluto.

“Mickey’s ears and white gloves, Minnie’s bow, Goofy’s playful silhouette – they’re instantly recognisable shapes, and that made them really fun to work with,” Westman told Dezeen about working with the familiar characters.

American architect Steven Holl has designed a colourful watch for Swiss watch brand Cauny informed by a compliment architect Álvaro Siza once gave him, telling Holl he used colour “like Matisse”.

The colourful watch, which has a three-dimensional dial with red, green, yellow and blue colour blocks, was designed to be a dialogue between the two architects.

A housing development in Andorra designed by French studio Ateliers Jean Nouvel and Spanish studio Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos has been damaged in a fire.

Called La Querola, the project is shortlisted in the housing category of this year’s Dezeen Awards and recently won the awards’ public vote. The cause of the fire is unknown and no official estimate of the extent of the damage has been released so far.

In Shanghai, access to the staircase of the Grand Opera House by international studio Snøhetta has been restricted to ticket holders.

Access to the spiral staircase, which leads up to the roof and has become a popular spot for photos, now costs £5.60 per person. Snøhetta told Dezeen that “visitor management is necessary”.

In car news, Swedish brand Polestar has unveiled its Formula 2030 concept car that the brand notes “screams performance”.

The low-slung sports car has signature Dual Blade headlights and was intended to project power, with a long bonnet, wraparound windscreen, short overhangs, muscular haunches and 22-inch wheels.

In a roundup, we explored five examples of Mesoamerican modern architecture that combine principles from ancient architecture with modern techniques.

Curator and writer Su Wu chose five homes, which she says “reflect the complex aesthetic cultures of Mesoamerica”, from her book on the subject.

Popular projects on Dezeen this week include a former agricultural barn in Cornwall, a viewpoint informed by Viking rings and a playful Portuguese retreat.

  • The Mitakon Speedmaster 65mm f/1.4 II is lighter than its predecessor, has a latest aperture diaphragm, and features an upgraded metal design.
  • It has been revealed that the optical design is unchanged, with the lens still sporting 11 elements arranged across seven groups.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, way back in 2018, Zhongyi (ZY) Optics rolled out the Mitakon Speedmaster 65mm f/1.4 manual-focus lens for the Fujifilm GFX mirrorless camera system. Now there’s an upgraded Mark II version, which is still ultra-fast, manual-focus, and very affordable. It’s also available for Hasselblad cameras.

The Mitakon Speedmaster 65mm f/1.4 II is lighter than its predecessor, has a latest aperture diaphragm, and features an upgraded metal design.

It has been revealed that the optical design is unchanged, with the lens still sporting 11 elements arranged across seven groups. ZY Optics notes the lens, which has two High Refractive Index (HRI) and two Ultra-Low Dispersion (UD) elements, delivers “exceptional image quality” with minimized chromatic aberrations.

However, behind the glass is a fresh 11-bladed aperture diaphragm, up from a nine-bladed unit in the original Speedmaster 65mm f/1.4. ZY Optics claims the new circular diaphragm delivers “rounder bokeh highlights.”.

In a recent development, with its f/1.4 aperture, the lens is still among the very fastest available for the Fujifilm GFX system. Fujifilm itself doesn’t make any lenses quite as fast—its fastest options are the GF 55mm f/1.7 R WR and the GF 80mm f/1.7, both of which cost over $2,000.

Sources indicate that over on the Hasselblad X system, it’s a similar story. Hasselblad’s fastest lens is the XCD 1,9/80, or, put in more common terms, an 80mm f/1.9 lens. The tech giant’s 65mm prime is the XCD 2,8/65.

Industry observers note that granted, Fujifilm’s and Hasselblad’s lenses are also native and equipped with autofocus, so there’s that. ZY Optics targets a different market, one less concerned with autofocus and looking to save some money.

The manual-focus prime can focus as close as 0.7 meters (2.3 feet), resulting in a maximum magnification of about 0.25x. Its 65mm focal length delivers a full-frame equivalent of just over 51mm.

Industry observers note that compared to its predecessor, the Mark II lens is significantly lighter. Weighing 900 grams (31.7 ounces), it sheds about 150 grams (5.3 ounces) compared to the original. The lens measures 95 millimeters (3.74 inches) long, accepts a 67mm filter thread, and features a built-in retractable lens hood.

ZY Optics indicates the fresh lens has an improved, precision-machined metal barrel. It looks a little different overall but retains the same general design, with a wide, ridged focus ring and an aperture control ring near the front of the lens. The depth-of-field scale markings have changed slightly, too.

The ZY Optics Mitakon Speedmaster 65mm f/1.4 II is available now for Fujifilm GFX and Hasselblad X mounts for $599.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Regional Canon offices worldwide have issued an urgent service notice regarding the manufacturer’s RF1.4x and RF2x extenders, commonly known as teleconverters. Canon warns that if users suspect anything unusual about how their extender feels in use, they should request an inspection and repair through Canon.

Canon Rumors claims this is a known glitch with Canon RF-mount extenders, where a lens can feel like it is locked onto the extender even when it isn’t. In some cases, a lens could even detach from the extender and fall to the ground. Given that extenders are commonly used with expensive telephoto lenses, this could be an extremely costly problem.

In a recent development, canon Malaysia’s notice on the matter is particularly interesting, offering slightly more information than the service notice from Canon U.S.A. and others.

“We regret to inform that a potential issue has been confirmed for Extender RF1.4x/RF2x,” Canon Malaysia notes, which goes further than what Canon U.S.A. writes.

Industry observers note that canon U.S.A. stops short of mentioning any concern, only issuing a “service notice” and noting that Canon RF extender users should always check the following:.

Canon U.S.A. adds that if photographers notice “anything unusual,” which could include the lens release lever feeling “stiff” or like it is “catching on something and cannot be operated smoothly,” there is a chance the RF lens is not locked in place.

“If used in this state, the RF lens may come off,” Canon continues.

Any affected users, or those who have any concerns about the operation of their RF extenders, should contact the Canon Customer Support Center in their region for an inspection and, if necessary, a free repair.

It has been revealed that in any case, it is not immediately clear what the exact concern is, what causes it, or how it might be fixed. Given that Canon is offering free repairs, though, it is reasonable to speculate that there is a physical component that needs to be fixed to ensure the consistently safe operation of Canon RF extenders.

According to recent reports, any photographers with Canon RF extenders should carefully inspect them before use and, if worried at all, contact their local Canon customer support team. A lens falling off an extender is a significant risk.

PetaPixel has reached out to Canon for comment and will enhancement this story if it hears back.

Mexico's Parque del Jaguar protects jaguars with 18-kilometre limestone wall

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (546 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mexican studio Colectivo C733 has created an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through while protecting more than 1,000 hectares of forest at Parque del Jaguar in Tulum, Mexico.
  • The project aims to safeguard one of the region’s vital habitats for jaguars, whose movement through the landscape had become disrupted by roads, development and tourism.
  • Rather than creating a conventional enclosed nature reserve, Colectivo C733 designed a network of boundaries, access points and visitor facilities intended to protect the animals‘ habitat while allowing people to explore the area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Rafael Gamo.

Mexican studio Colectivo C733 has created an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through while protecting more than 1,000 hectares of forest at Parque del Jaguar in Tulum, Mexico.

The project aims to safeguard one of the region’s vital habitats for jaguars, whose movement through the landscape had become disrupted by roads, development and tourism.

Rather than creating a conventional enclosed nature reserve, Colectivo C733 designed a network of boundaries, access points and visitor facilities intended to protect the animals‘ habitat while allowing people to explore the area.

The park occupies a coastal territory containing tropical forest, mangroves, underground rivers and karstic geology, as well as the ancient Mayan archaeological site of Tulum.

Its landscape had also been affected by contaminated soil around a former airstrip and habitat disruption caused by the Cancún-Tulum highway.

At its perimeter, the studio added an 18-kilometre dry-stacked limestone wall, known locally as a tecorral, informed by traditional Mayan stone boundaries.

Built without mortar, the wall allows wildlife to move through gaps between the stones while establishing a physical boundary around the protected area.

Within the park, Colectivo C733 introduced a number of public buildings and viewing platforms, concentrating upcoming construction in previously altered areas and leaving large sections of the territory untouched.

Low-impact transport routes, including pedestrian and cycling paths, connect the different areas, with electric transport also introduced to reduce the impact of visitor movement.

The routes link the park’s public facilities with its archaeological and ecological sites.

At the central entrance, a timber-framed building is screened by closely spaced vertical wooden members and topped with a woven palm-thatch roof.

The complex accommodates a museum, cafe, shop, multipurpose room and open-air forum, alongside a kitchen designed for cooking over smoke.

Other structures include elevated observation towers and a long suspended walkway that crosses the forest canopy, revealing different aspects of the area’s geology, water systems and biodiversity as visitors move through it.

“By designing how the territory is revealed, inhabited, and understood over time, Parque del Jaguar shifts architecture from a static intervention to an evolving framework that connects environment, culture, and collective awareness,” Colectivo C733 stated.

Access is more controlled in sensitive areas, helping to limit disturbance to wildlife habitats, including those used by jaguars.

At the coast, stone platforms, stepped seating and raised timber staircases provide access to viewpoints overlooking the Caribbean Sea.

The buildings use locally sourced limestone, chicozapote timber, sascab – a naturally occurring limestone-based material – and palm thatch.

Green roofs, shaded outdoor spaces and naturally ventilated structures help reduce the need for mechanical cooling in the tropical climate.

Alongside the construction work, the project includes soil remediation, reforestation and the recovery of natural water systems.

Asphalt has been removed from previously developed areas as part of efforts to restore the ground and reconnect habitats.

Founded in 2019, Colectivo C733 brings together the practices of Gabriela Carrillo, Carlos Facio, José Amozurrutia, Eric Valdez and Israel Espín to work on public architecture and urban infrastructure across Mexico.

Its other projects featured on Dezeen include a square-shaped pedestrian pier that hovers over a lagoon in Bacalar, Mexico and a brick music school topped with a cantilevered coconut wood roof in Nacajuca, Mexico.

Photography by Rafael Gamo.

It has been revealed that (Not Boring) Camera is one of three finalists for iPhone App of the Year, and it’s easy to see why. The app, sometimes stylized as !Camera, features a fully 3D camera interface, extensive customization, and haptic feedback designed to replicate the feel of holding an actual camera.

“You’re gonna love how it feels,” indicates the app’s developer, Not Boring. “I guarantee it.”.

In a recent development, (Not Boring) Camera aims to be more than just a pretty face, though. Like other popular iPhone camera apps released in recent years, !Camera eschews AI processing in favor of a more natural imaging engine. Its proprietary SuperRaw mode promises “film-like tones” while preserving a photo’s “beautiful natural grain.”.

The app supports Apple’s ProRAW and Basic processing, plus it can save photos as RAW DNG files for editing in other apps, like Darkroom, Lightroom, and Photoshop. It also supports HDR image capture across four settings: off, low, medium, and high.

“!Camera is the first camera app to enable professional-level color grading with 3D LUTs (‘lookup tables’) used in high-end workflows by pro photographers to achieve realistic film simulations and unique cinematic looks,” Not Boring continues. The app includes photographer-designed LUTs, LUT importing, and preset creation tools. The firm regularly releases new styles and collaborations.

Industry observers note that the most recent collaboration is with the Tokyo-based art collective Nuevo.Tokyo. The AgBr style brings a vintage-inspired black-and-white look to !Camera.

Sources indicate that the app also packs extensive manual controls—including exposure, shutter speed, white balance, ISO, and focus—alongside tools like focus peaking, zebra stripes, and a histogram. For finer focus adjustments, the virtual lens features its own “Precision Focus Ring” with a focus scale.

Sources indicate that customization extends to the look of the camera app itself. People can design a custom virtual camera by choosing colors for its body, top panel, lens, and buttons.

It has been revealed that if (Not Boring) Camera ultimately wins the award when winners are confirmed next month, it certainly won’t be the first camera app to earn the honor. In 2024, Kino and Adobe Lightroom were both honored among Apple’s Apps of the Year. Halide Mark II won in 2022, too.

(Not Boring) Camera is available now for free. Access to all features requires a Plus membership, which is $14.99 per year or $59.99 for a lifetime license.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for audiences who associate the US photographer Nan Goldin with the friends and lovers of her slideshow The Ballad of Sexual Dependency (1973-86), her forthcoming Hayward Gallery exhibition may come as a surprise. Animals, a solar eclipse and footage salvaged from nature documentaries will feature in Goldin’s first institutional solo show in the UK since her 2002 retrospective at the Whitechapel Gallery.

What links these subjects to the photographs that established her reputation? According to the Hayward’s chief curator, Rachel Thomas, the connection lies in the relationships Goldin creates through the camera, rather than the identities of those who appear before it. In Thomas’s reading, Goldin’s focus on queer communities and chosen family has widened to embrace the natural world.

Nan Goldin, Still from You never did anything wrong, Part II, 2026.

© Nan Goldin, courtesy the artist and Gagosian.

Industry observers note that rather than being a retrospective, the exhibition You Never Did Anything Wrong presents new and recent work by Goldin. Thomas, who worked with the photographer at the Irish Museum of Modern Art in 2017, tells The Art Newspaper: “I wanted to collaborate again to reveal where her practice is moving now.” Four years in the making, the exhibition is the Hayward’s contribution to the Southbank Centre’s 75th-anniversary programme devoted to “visionaries who have fundamentally redefined culture”.

According to recent reports, the show’s centrepiece will be the premiere of You never did anything wrong, Part II (2026). Created with the film-maker David Sherman, it draws on 16mm nature documentaries from the 1960s and 70s, and damaged soundtracks from old films, with a new score by the British musician Mica Levi. Goldin turns material associated with explaining the natural world into an abstract meditation on animals, land and impending extinction.

Nan Goldin, Still from You never did anything wrong, Part I, 2024.

© Nan Goldin, courtesy the artist and Gagosian.

According to recent reports, it accompanies You never did anything wrong, Part I (2024), which centres on a solar eclipse and draws on a myth of animals stealing the sun. Together, the films bring Goldin’s work into a world without human protagonists.

In a recent development, elsewhere, Stendhal Syndrome (2024), receiving its UK premiere, places photographs of her friends and lovers in dialogue with classical art, accompanied by a score by Soundwalk Collective. Memory Lost (2019-21), meanwhile, returns to addiction, connecting personal experience to Goldin’s campaigning with Pain (Prescription Addiction Intervention Now), the group she founded to confront the opioid crisis in the US.

Art of intimacy: Young Love (2024) is one of Goldin’s works in Stendhal Syndrome © Nan Goldin; courtesy the artist and Gagosian.

Industry observers note that for Thomas, compassion connects these changing subjects. Goldin’s importance lies partly in her refusal to maintain a distance from the people she photographs, with the exhibition proposing that this approach can extend beyond her own community. “What endures across every medium and chapter is an exploration of compassion,” Thomas says. “Goldin simply expands the horizon of who and what is embraced by her gaze.”.

• You Never Did Anything Wrong, Hayward Gallery, London, 24 November-14 March 2027.

Discircle builds the Lemonade Global Ventures brand identity on a gold lemon globe, Zero Sugar discipline, and a black and acid yellow system.

Recent findings suggest that the whole system starts with one image: a lemon cast in gold, its pitted peel catching the light on pure black. Discircle, a studio from Curitiba, built the identity for Lemonade Global Ventures, an investment fund founded by entrepreneurs, backing profitable businesses with proven cash generation. The mark fuses the lemon with a globe: a calculated elliptical profile, its longitudinal lines reading as citrus segments and as earth meridians at the same time. Gold carries the value, black the weight, acid yellow the shouting. The studio calls the approach Zero Sugar, paired with Squeeze: growth demands sour decisions, an appetite for risk, and no easy formulas.

Industry observers note that the type does the talking in a tight grotesque with close tracking. Headlines run large and blunt: HOW TO MATURE on the book cover, Investment Perspective across the report, Squeeze the Extraordinary beside the steel squeezer. Small caps do the quiet work underneath: MADE WITH BRAZILIAN LEMONS, POTENTIAL, CONCENTRATED, GROWTH REPORT. The LGV monogram sits beside the line drawn lemon globe.

Recent findings suggest that the grid stays strict. Report A runs on three columns, Diagnosis, Strategy, Execution, each with the same measure, and the same three moves return as L1, L2, L3: structural diagnosis and expansion vectors, organization and leverage, consolidation and scale. Each stage gets a white oval and a pill label at the bottom, AGO, SET, OUT. Type sits on generous black space, so a few lines read louder than a full page.

It has been revealed that the finishes stay physical. The gold lemon is a solid object, peel texture and all. The same mark turns into a gold lapel pin, its meridian lines cut into polished metal, on a black suit lapel. Report A pairs an acid yellow front and a grey board back, the letters L, G and V large at the corners, with inside pages showing the paper grain. The squeezer in the closing frame is a real steel object, ribbed and reflective.

The system stretches without thinning. Brazil becomes a map of gold lemons under the line Tropical Capital. The Lemonade Makers wall lists fifteen names, from Martin Luther King Jr. to Oscar Wilde, separated by small yellow lemons, with the line Lemonade Makers squeeze the real greatness running underneath. The book How to Mature carries the same headline and mark, and the report keeps the same discipline.

Lumix Has the Video Chops to Beat Sony, So Why Won’t It Even Try?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1077 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
