  • In a recent development, for context, this year is the 25th anniversary of the Lumix brand, and the organization opened with the L10 back in May.
  • Recent findings suggest that and so I carried that excitement with me for the next six months, knowing we might not see that promise come to fruition until late fall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A couple of weeks ago, Jordan Drake texted me from the Lumix event in Osaka with the rundown on what was being declared. When he described the S1 II but in a box camera format, I couldn’t help but express my dismay. “That’s it?”.

In a recent development, for context, this year is the 25th anniversary of the Lumix brand, and the organization opened with the L10 back in May. That felt like a proper start to what we assumed would be a full year of serious product introduces. This wasn’t an expectation we came in with; it was one that Lumix put into our heads: the company specifically said it had more planned for 2026 and that we should be excited.

Recent findings suggest that and so I carried that excitement with me for the next six months, knowing we might not see that promise come to fruition until late fall. That is a major reason why I’m so disappointed by the SHX1. It’s not that the camera is bad or that it doesn’t have a core, dedicated audience. It’s more that this isn’t the camera that I was expecting to be the cap of a celebratory year where Lumix was poised to really strut its stuff.

Industry observers note that the Lumix S1H has been languishing for years, and not because there isn’t a market for it. It just seems like Panasonic doesn’t know what to do with it. When the S1 II was announced last year, that really felt like the case because the camera felt like it did everything we ever wanted the S1H successor to do.

But I argue that, even with all that known, Lumix — the brand known for video performance — has, for some reason, been unwilling to take on Sony in the highly competitive commercial camera space that is dominated by the FX series. For all of its strengths in video, Lumix appears scared: either of Sony or of the success that would come from actually trying.

In 2021, Sony announced the FX3 and, in one fell swoop, changed the game. It created the perfect camera for the mid- to high-end filmmaker at a really compelling sub-$4,000 price. It wasn’t part of the Alpha series, so Sony could fully focus on video performance. The FX3 is the logical conclusion to the success that the a7S series created, and it was (and still is) immensely popular.

As Jordan Drake put it in this week’s episode of The PetaPixel Podcast, the FX3 became the industry standard through its design.

It has been revealed that “It became just the industry standard for if you’re doing event work or commercial work. Because it is such a recognizable camera – like that gray, with that pronounced, sharp-edged grip – when producers and directors and people see it, they immediately know that’s acceptable. That’s the big thing I think Panasonic’s butting up against. An S1 II is every bit as capable but it looks like an old DSLR. And I think everybody wants to move away from that,” he claims.

“The FX3 is just the visual language of a semi-professional small camera now.”.

Canon and Nikon got that memo, which is why the ZR and the R6V have that same visual design language. Panasonic Lumix has chosen to ignore that aspect of its cameras to its extreme detriment.

Sources indicate that compared to Sony, Panasonic’s camera division (it is now one division that combined Lumix and VariCam) is small, and maybe that’s to blame for these concerns. Maybe it doesn’t have a good design department. That would make sense, since Lumix has not been a particularly good example of enticing camera design, and it’s very much hurting it now. I think it believes it should be able to stand out through performance alone, and that’s a lovely sentiment, but it’s just not reality.

Industry observers note that creators buy cameras that they want to be seen with, not just cameras that can do the job. You can argue that isn’t how it should be, but it is very much a reality.

It has been revealed that there is nothing wrong with the SHX1. It’s an excellent camera that will resonate with current Lumix filmmakers. Maybe that’s what Lumix wants: to keep its current audience happy.

It has been revealed that but that’s not what Lumix needs right now. To grow and find itself in more hands, Lumix needs to actually beat Sony at its own game – a game it is entirely equipped to win handily. I am a Lumix user and have been since the GH4. It’s reluctance to even try and take on the FX tier is incredibly disheartening, because I 100% would love to have an FX5-styled camera with Lumix guts.

According to recent reports, lumix’s in-body stabilization is better. Lumix’s record modes are, on the whole, better. I mean, the company was giving filmmakers open gate and in-camera anamorphic desqueeze years before it was even a twinkle in the other brands’ eyes. This is the space where Lumix should be king, but its refusal to go at Sony head-on makes it seem like the company is scared it might not succeed.

Or, worse, Lumix is scared of the success that would bring it. Maybe it doesn’t want that level of attention. Maybe it likes feeling like a scrappy underdog, and the idea of being a market leader is just too much pressure.

Whatever the case, as good as the SHX1 is, it’s not the camera Lumix needed to release in this moment. Sony was stumbling and tripping over itself with the FX5 launch, giving Lumix the perfect window to jump ahead if it were prepared for the moment. It clearly was not.

I get not being able to directly respond to the FX5, but the FX3? Five years later, how do you not respond to that? You, the video camera manufacturer? It feels like cowardice despite the timing not possibly being any better… which makes missing that moment even worse.

I don’t think Lumix fully grasps how badly they fumbled this opportunity. They might not realize the extent of this mistake for months or years. With the moment up for grabs, Lumix just chose not to reach out for it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tree trunks puncture the slim timber platforms of this minimalist sauna in a Japanese woodland, designed by local architecture studio Daichi Inc.

Named Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna, the project is nestled within a forest in Kanagawa, southwest of Tokyo, and forms part of the Daichi Silent River retreat alongside guest cabins and additional sauna spaces.

According to Daichi Inc, the idea for the project was to make the trees feel “part of the architecture itself”, using them as both supports and the defining feature of the pared-back structure.

The sauna has been shortlisted in the Leisure and wellness category of Dezeen Awards 2026.

“Conventional architecture typically clears nature away, cutting down thick and strong trees and transforming them into standardised building materials,” said the studio.

“In this project, however, the existing trees were preserved and used directly as part of the spatial framework, blurring the boundary between nature and the built environment,” it added.

“Rather than placing architecture on top of nature, the project allows architecture to coexist with it, creating an immersive bodily experience in which people feel as though they are dissolving into the forest itself.”.

Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna’s structure comprises two stacked timber decks and a roof, with the central platform partially supported by the site’s natural slope.

The thin planes sit atop timber grids supported by the trees themselves and punctured by small circular cut-outs through which their trunks can grow.

Recent findings suggest that timber steps connect these different platforms, culminating on the upper level where the central sauna room sits, wrapped in frameless glass panels. It contains a wooden bench and a central log burner.

Aside from the sauna room and a small plunge pool, the decks are left entirely open and flexible, and are surrounded by slender metal balustrades at their edges.

“Wood and glass were used as the primary materials, while the existing trees themselves were integrated into the architectural framework,” noted the studio.

According to recent reports, “Decks and sauna spaces were carefully positioned to appear as if floating within the forest,” it added. “The forest is not treated as a backdrop, but functions as an essential structural part of the architecture itself.

Other saunas recently featured on Dezeen include Puusauna in Finland by architect Jaakko Torvinen, which is supported by whole, charred tree trunks sourced from the neighbouring forest, and an off-grid bathhouse in London.

The $30,000 average wedding figure you see everywhere is misleading. That number is skewed upward by luxury weddings in expensive metros like Upcoming York, San Francisco, and Los Angeles. The national median — the number where half of weddings cost more and half cost less — sits closer to $10,000 to $15,000. That distinction matters because it means a beautiful, memorable wedding is absolutely possible without spending five figures you do not have.

Recent findings suggest that the FI perspective adds another layer: every dollar spent on a wedding is a dollar that cannot compound for decades. A $30,000 wedding invested for 30 years at a 7% average annual return grows to roughly $228,000. That does not mean you should elope in a courthouse (unless you want to), but it does mean you should spend intentionally on the categories that matter most to you and cut ruthlessly everywhere else.

Here is where the typical wedding dollar goes:.

The biggest takeaway from this table: venue and catering are 60-70% of the total. If you can reduce those two categories, you change the entire math.

Not all wedding spending creates equal memories. Research consistently demonstrates that couples remember three things most vividly years later: the ceremony itself, the food and drinks, and the photographs. Almost nobody remembers the chair covers, the napkin folds, or the custom monogram on the cocktail napkins.

That insight creates a clear FI-aligned strategy: splurge on what creates lasting memories (photographer, food, music) and minimize everything else.

Sources indicate that the golden rule of wedding budgeting: if you cannot remember whether a detail was present at the last three weddings you attended, your guests will not notice either. Cut it without guilt.

It has been revealed that the biggest financial mistake couples make is not setting a firm budget before visiting any vendors. Venues and vendors are skilled at upselling, and without a hard number in mind, costs spiral promptly. Start with a number you can pay in cash — wedding debt is one of the worst ways to begin a marriage and a direct threat to your FI timeline.

Follow this payment timeline to manage cash flow without credit card debt:.

A practical savings strategy: divide your total budget by the number of months until the wedding and automate that transfer to a dedicated savings account. If your budget is $15,000 and your wedding is 15 months away, that is $1,000 per month. Treat it like any other savings goal on your FI path — automate, do not touch, and watch it grow.

For couples on the FI path, consider this reframe: every dollar you shave from the wedding budget is a dollar that starts compounding immediately. Cutting $5,000 from a $20,000 wedding and investing that savings at 7% for 25 years creates roughly $27,000 in future wealth. You can have a wonderful wedding and build wealth simultaneously — but only if you plan intentionally from the start.

Industry observers note that before finalizing your wedding budget, run the compound interest math on any amount you are considering spending. A $30,000 wedding invested at 7% for 30 years becomes roughly $228,000. A $15,000 wedding invested at 7% for 30 years becomes roughly $114,000. This is not an argument against celebrating — it is an argument for spending intentionally on what matters to you and cutting everything else. The couple who spends $15,000 on a joyful celebration and invests the other $15,000 gets both the wedding and a significant head start on financial independence.

According to recent reports, there is no single right number, but the median US wedding cost of $10,000 to $15,000 is achievable for most couples without going into debt. Focus on what matters most to you and cut everything else. A $10,000 wedding with great food, a good photographer, and people you love is better than a $30,000 wedding that starts your marriage with financial stress.

Sources indicate that no. Wedding debt is one of the worst forms of consumer debt because it funds a single day with no residual asset value. The average couple who finances their wedding on credit cards at 22% interest turns a $20,000 wedding into a $28,000 expense over 4 years of payments. Set a cash budget and stick to it.

Any contribution from parents is a gift, not an obligation. If parents offer to contribute, have an honest conversation about the total amount and whether it comes with expectations about the guest list or style. Budget based on what you can afford independently, then treat any parental contribution as a bonus.

Recent findings suggest that yes. Friday and Sunday weddings typically cost 20-30% less than Saturday weddings for the same venue and vendors. Some venues offer discounts of 40% or more for weekday weddings (Monday through Thursday). Off-season months like January, February, March, and November also offer significant savings.

Sources indicate that tips for vendors (proposal 15-20% for catering staff, bartenders, and drivers), alterations for wedding attire ($200-$500), marriage license fees ($30-$100), and overtime charges if the reception runs past the contracted time. Build a 10% contingency buffer into your total budget for these surprises.

Set your budget privately as a couple before discussing with family. Present it as a decision, not a discussion. If family members want upgrades, they are welcome to fund those specific additions. Protect your financial foundation — the marriage matters more than the wedding, and starting debt-free sets up your partnership for success.

A meaningful wedding does not require $30,000 or any specific dollar amount. Set a cash budget based on what you can afford without debt, allocate spending toward what creates lasting memories (food, photography, people), and cut everything else. Every dollar you save on the wedding is a dollar that starts compounding toward your financial independence. The couples with the strongest financial futures are the ones who celebrate joyfully within their means and invest the difference.

Fujifilm has unveiled that it will host an X Summit in Paris on December 2 at 4 AM EST. X Summits have traditionally been Fujifilm’s stage for announcing a new product, and given Fujifilm has not released an X-series camera this year, it could very much use one.

“2026 is stated to mark 200 years since the invention of photography in France,” Fujifilm notes. “To celebrate two centuries of photographic history, and to honor all the photographers and photography lovers who have created countless inspiring images along the way, the next X Summit comes to you from Paris, France.”.

Fujifilm has not hosted an X Summit in 2026, although it has hosted multiple Fujikina events around the world, including in Denmark and Poland this past spring and in Upcoming York City in October. The last X Summit was held in Shanghai in June 2025, which saw the announcement of the X-E5 and 23mm f/2.8 R. Before that, the X Summit in Prague launched the GFX100RF.

Going 18 months between X Summits is extremely unusual, but getting one in 2026 at all feels like a gift, given how quiet Fujifilm has been this year.

There is no official word on what to expect out of this X Summit (of course), although the perception has been that Fujifilm’s flagship cameras are in dire need of a refresh: the X-Pro, X-T, and X-H cameras are long in the tooth now.

In a recent development, A new camera launch would also be an opportunity to address the largest complaint Fujifilm has come up against: autofocus. To its credit, Fujifilm knows it’s a place it must improve.

“We’re trying,” Yuji Igarashi, General Manager of Professional Imaging Group, Imaging Solutions Division, Fujifilm Corporation, explained to PetaPixel at CP+ 2026 in Yokohama. “We still believe it’s necessary to just continue to improve by algorithm improvement. And it’s not that we’re not doing it. We are continuing to work on it.”.

Speaking of future devices, Igarashi said improved sensors and processors likely would help.

“In theory, future devices will be much more advanced, with the consideration of higher processing speed. That would help us as well, but that wouldn’t help existing people, so we’re trying to do both — algorithm improvement plus device improvement.”.

Fujifilm will broadcast the X Summit live on its YouTube channel on December 2 at 4 AM EST.

Obsbot has revealed the Tail 2 ADV, a newly introduced 4K PTZR camera featuring a 21x optical zoom and custom LUT support.

The camera, which has already earned a 2027 CES Innovation Award, features a custom Type 1/2 image sensor with Dual Native ISO and support for 4Kp60 and 1080p120 recording.

Obsbot says the camera’s AI-powered image signal processing pipeline handles noise reduction and enables 4K HDR video at up to 30p with all-pixel phase-detect autofocus.

“All-pixel PDAF and Focus Over Zooming help the camera rapidly refocus on distant, stationary subjects as focal length changes during a zoom,” Obsbot says.

Recent findings suggest that speaking of zooming, the Tail 2 ADV’s lens has an equivalent focal length range of 34-702mm and a variable aperture system. At the wide end, the aperture ranges from f/1.7 to f/7, while for telephoto shooting, it ranges from f/3.8 to f/7.

In Pro mode, camera operators can remotely adjust aperture, ISO, and shutter speed, offering greater creative control in changing lighting conditions such as stage performances, outdoor productions, and houses of worship.

It has been revealed that the camera includes built-in subject recognition for autofocus tracking, identifying people, more than 30 animal species, and over 200 object categories. Using its pan, tilt, and zoom capabilities, it can automatically adjust framing to keep moving subjects in view. Operators can choose from six tracking speed settings alongside custom modes, as well as define preferred framing and tracking boundaries.

Industry observers note that “These settings allow live production teams to determine not just which subject the camera follows, but how it executes the shot,” Obsbot explains. The camera can also roll thanks to its built-in gimbal, enabling native 4Kp60 vertical recording without cropping.

For professional workflows, the Tail 2 ADV offers Obsbot Log—a proprietary logarithmic image profile that promises greater flexibility during color grading—alongside custom LUT support. Consumers can import and preview custom LUTs in Obsbot’s accompanying software, and the camera supports timecode and Precision Time Protocol (PTP) to sync with other cameras.

For connectivity, the Obsbot Tail 2 ADV includes 3G-SDI output up to 1080p60 and a full-size HDMI 2.0 output supporting up to 4K resolution. It also features Gigabit Ethernet, a 2.5mm RS-232 port, two USB-C ports, separate 3.5mm mic and line inputs, and a microSD card slot. The camera’s built-in 5,000mAh battery delivers over four and a half hours of operation, while USB PD 3.0 and PoE+ support allow for extended continuous power.

The Obsbot Tail 2 ADV PTZR camera will arrive on December 8. Preorders are open now with a limited-time $200 discount, bringing the price down from its $1,599 MSRP to $1,399.

  • According to recent reports, the Sotheby’s statement records that the auction house is “pleased to confirm that an agreement has been reached between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and all of the legal descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer regarding the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs”.
  • The work is estimated at around $180m ($207m with fees) and has been guaranteed by Sotheby's to sell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, sotheby’s today announced that a settlement has been reached over the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890). The work has been poised to achieve a record price for the artist but became the subject of a claim by the heirs of its Jewish former owners, who called for the work to be withdrawn from the 18 November auction in Fresh York.

According to recent reports, the Sotheby’s statement records that the auction house is “pleased to confirm that an agreement has been reached between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and all of the legal descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer regarding the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs”. The sale will now proceed as planned.

The work is estimated at around $180m ($207m with fees) and has been guaranteed by Sotheby's to sell. This is far in excess of the previous record of $117m, paid at Christie’s in 2022 for Van Gogh’s Orchard with Cypresses (April 1888).

The Blaquier-Arrieta family, from Argentina, bought Blossoming Chestnut Trees in 1975. As the Sotheby’s statement explains: “In recognition of the painting’s complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement.”.

Industry observers note that the provenance in the Sotheby’s catalogue entry notes, as it has done since last month, that the painting was acquired by the Berlin publisher Samuel Fischer and his wife Hedwig in 1909. Their son-in-law, Gottfried Bermann Fischer, deposited the Van Gogh with the Amsterdam gallery Paul Cassirer in 1932 or 1933—and it was then bought by Paris collectors Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in 1936.

Industry observers note that last Thursday (12 November), in a surprise move, the Berlin-based restitution researcher Gunnar Schnabel sent a letter to Sotheby’s, on behalf of the Fischer heirs. He questioned the 1936 sale—which he says took place three months after the family had left Berlin for Vienna—asking Sotheby’s to prove that the picture had been sold at its market value and that its sale was not forced. In the meantime, Schnabel asked for this week’s sale to be delayed.

In a statement, the Fischer heirs commented: “We are grateful for the trusting and fair negotiation and collaboration with Sotheby’s and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which make it possible to acknowledge the suffering of the Fischer family during the Nazi era and honour Gisela Berman Fischer's [granddaughter of Samuel and Hedwig] history of seeking justice for her family.”.

According to recent reports, the Blaquier-Arrieta family commented: “We are pleased to have reached an amicable resolution with the Fischer heirs. We appreciate the constructive dialogue that made this resolution possible and look forward to an extraordinary result and to passing along this masterpiece to a upcoming generation of collectors.”.

No details have been released on the nature of the agreement and whether the Fischer family will receive financial compensation.

What impact, if any, the short-lived dispute will have on the sale will only become apparent with the bidding.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.
  • The customisable textile – named Bianni – was made by weaving together wool with recycled paper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mexican design studio Arudeko has developed Bianni, a paper-like material made from colourful waste wool, which can be sculpted into everything from lampshades to room dividers.

Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.

The customisable textile – named Bianni – was made by weaving together wool with recycled paper.

Skilled local artisans initially wove the discarded dyed wool onto a pedal loom, then, using cotton threads, wove strips of recycled paper crafted by local papermakers into the material.

The result is a translucent, flexible textile that can be crafted into diverse objects, from lampshades to decorative headboard panels, room dividers and wall art.

“Through exploring the material’s qualities, we discovered its potential, particularly the way light revealed colours that had been hidden within the paper, almost like a secret waiting to be uncovered,” Arudeko co-founder and CEO Denisse Arnaiz told Dezeen.

“Once the paper was woven, I began observing how it behaved as a textile,” added Arnaiz.

“Its translucency was what ultimately inspired us to explore its use in lighting. However, the material has many other possible applications.”.

With Bianni, Arudeko aimed to uncover the hidden value of discarded wool whilst reimagining the ancient material’s ancestral history and “cultural memory”.

It has been revealed that “Bianni was born from the idea of giving latest life to the leftover wool from our rug and cushion production in Oaxaca,” mentioned Arnaiz. “This wool carries within it the knowledge of the artisans who work with it, as well as the colours of the earth embedded in its fibres.”.

Arnaiz explained that the material is made purely from natural materials, with no additives.

“No additives, just natural materials – why mix these fibres?” she said. “Not only for an aesthetic purpose, as wool brings fire resistance to the paper.”.

It has been revealed that throughout the process, the studio aimed to minimise water consumption and carbon dioxide production as much as possible. Bianni’s production was also kept local to reduce transport needs whilst supporting the local community.

By working with artisans from rural communities and blending traditional craft knowledge with contemporary design practice, Bianni aims to champion historic crafts whilst fostering long-term community development and economic inclusion.

Other wool projects recently featured on Dezeen include waste-wool cladding designed for retrofits and a collection of rugs with architectural designs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Instagram has introduced a new feature that allows customers to edit Stories after publishing them without losing existing views, likes, or replies.

Confirmed by Instagram head Adam Mosseri, the revision gives users a 15-minute window to change text, music, stickers, and drawings after sharing a Story.

Previously, customers had to delete and repost a Story to correct a typo, change its caption, or add music they had forgotten to include. The new feature removes that requirement, allowing edits to be made while preserving the post’s existing engagement.

The Verge notes that the ability to edit Stories was first spotted in development by reverse engineer Alessandro Paluzzi in April. It is now rolling out to users. To make changes, users can open a published Story, select the three-dot menu in the bottom-right corner, and tap “Edit Story.” Edited posts will display an “edited” label when viewed by others.

A post shared by Adam Mosseri (@mosseri).

The change also addresses some of the complications associated with deleting and reposting Stories, particularly when they form part of a sequence. Re-uploading content can disrupt the original order of posts, while creators and social media managers may also be concerned about the impact of reposting on engagement metrics.

“A lot of people have been asking for this, so I’m excited to get this one out there,” Mosseri states.

It has been revealed that alongside the editing feature, Instagram is introducing several changes to its Stories tools. These include fresh fonts, colors, and shapes for stickers, which will be organized into sticker sheets to make them easier to browse. The platform is also updating its multiple-photo selection process and adding new background options, including blur effects, colors and gradients.

Yesterday, PetaPixel reported on Instagram’s newly introduced tool that’s designed to help creators on the platform protect their work.

Called content protection, it allows eligible creators to monitor copies of their videos across Instagram and Facebook and decide how to respond when a match is detected.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ellen von Unwerth, one of the most in-demand fashion photographers working today, claims there is no money left in the industry today.
  • For more than four decades, Von Unwerth has remained one of the most influential figures in fashion photography, widely recognized for her bold and playful images of women.
  • However, in an interview with Fashion Network France, Von Unwerth has revealed how the resources allocated to fashion photography have dramatically changed and how the industry is no longer as lucrative as it once was.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ellen von Unwerth, one of the most in-demand fashion photographers working today, claims there is no money left in the industry today.

For more than four decades, Von Unwerth has remained one of the most influential figures in fashion photography, widely recognized for her bold and playful images of women.

However, in an interview with Fashion Network France, Von Unwerth has revealed how the resources allocated to fashion photography have dramatically changed and how the industry is no longer as lucrative as it once was.

In a recent development, “These days, there’s no money left in fashion photography,” Von Unwerth tells Fashion Network France. “It’s nothing like it used to be, when there were 10 pages in magazines and newspapers, and posters everywhere. You don’t see that anymore. You don’t see the massive billboards anymore.”.

Industry observers note that von Unwerth explains that fashion photography has become less financially rewarding as brands increasingly direct their budgets toward events and influencers rather than traditional print ad campaigns. She claims photographers now face longer waits for payment, tighter deadlines, and less creative freedom than they had earlier in her career.

According to recent reports, “Now, the money goes into events, influencers… So there’s almost no money left,” she adds. “You have to wait a very long time to get paid. And then they want the photos tomorrow — or even yesterday! Before, we were on our own on set. It was really just us, the photographers. We were the bosses; we did our own thing. It was our kingdom; it was secret.”.

Recent findings suggest that von Unwerth indicates fashion photographers have increasingly lost control over their shoots, with multiple behind-the-scenes [BTS] photographers and teams now working on the same set. She says this makes it difficult to establish who actually took a particular image once it is published. She compares modern fashion shoots to film productions, where a director oversees several camera operators rather than capturing everything themselves.

According to recent reports, “Nowadays, there’s the BTS photographer. Then there are the BTS of the BTS. There are three other photographers doing different styles,” she tells Fashion Network France. “And I fought against that for a long time, but I’ve given up. Now there are five people taking pictures behind me. And you don’t know, when it comes out: “Is it my photo or is it someone else’s?” In the end, I just say it’s my photo! It’s like in the film industry: there’s a director, who oversees everything, and there are other cameramen filming.”.

Recalling a shoot for beauty brand L’Oréal, Von Unwerth says she became frustrated and ordered everyone to leave after discovering that around 50 people behind her were taking exactly the same photograph.

Von Unwerth’s comments come weeks after a report revealed that fashion photo studios are closing down as brands increasingly embrace AI thanks to the major savings offered by the technology.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A trial over the long-disputed estate of Andy Warhol’s photographer Billy Name, including the rights to his extensive photo archive, finally begins this week.
  • Name became Warhol’s close collaborator and photographer in the 1960s.
  • His Factory-era photographs are regarded as some of the most vital visual records of Warhol and the Pop Art movement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A trial over the long-disputed estate of Andy Warhol’s photographer Billy Name, including the rights to his extensive photo archive, finally begins this week.

Name became Warhol’s close collaborator and photographer in the 1960s. He lived in Warhol’s New York studio, the Factory, for seven years and became the artist’s in-house photographer. Using a Pentax Camera, Name captured thousands of iconic photos of Warhol, his art, and the stars who visited the Factory.

His Factory-era photographs are regarded as some of the most vital visual records of Warhol and the Pop Art movement.

Recent findings suggest that however, when Name — who was born William George Linich — died in 2016, a legal dispute broke out over his estate, which included the rights to his valuable collection of photographs. More than a decade after Name’s death, the rights and fate of thousands of his photographs still remain legally contested.

According to a report by Times Union, a new jury trial at Ulster County Surrogate’s Court in Ulster County, New York, will finally decide who has the right to license the black-and-white photographs Name took of Warhol and who will control the future of his extensive photo archive. The case will be the first jury trial over an estate that Ulster County Surrogate’s Court has ever presided over.

The dispute is between Name’s longtime friend and agent Dagon James and his niece Suzette Linich both of whom claim to be the photographer’s rightful heir. At the center of the legal battle are two different wills left by Name. Linich presented a will dated 2011 that named her as the executor and sole beneficiary of his estate. Although the court accepted the document, James subsequently presented a more recent will, signed in 2015, that left the entire estate to him.

A key question in the trial is whether Name had the mental capacity to make the 2015 will. By 2014, the photographer, who is in his early 70s, was reportedly suffering from arthritis, diabetes, and depression and was frequently hospitalized. Name’s family argues that he was often confused and vulnerable to influence, alleging that James persuaded the photographer to exclude his relatives from his will.

According to recent reports, james disputes those claims, maintaining that Name was mentally competent, trusted him, and made a deliberate decision to leave him in charge of his photographic legacy. The attorney who prepared the 2015 will testified that Name had clearly expressed his intention to exclude his relatives from his estate and leave everything to James.

Harvard museum returns human remains to Brazil

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Brazilian government held two ceremonies this month to mark the repatriation of the remains of two people of African descent taken from the country in the 19th century.
  • The repatriation is part of a university initiative launched in 2019 to review historical records related to individuals of African descent from Brazil and the Caribbean islands.
  • Sources indicate that the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (Museu Nacional/UFRJ) received the skull of an adult woman, held at the Peabody Museum since 1870 following its transfer from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Brazilian government held two ceremonies this month to mark the repatriation of the remains of two people of African descent taken from the country in the 19th century. The remains were transferred from the collection of Harvard University’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

The repatriation is part of a university initiative launched in 2019 to review historical records related to individuals of African descent from Brazil and the Caribbean islands. The review identified one person who is recorded as having been enslaved, while there is strong evidence that the other was as well.

Sources indicate that the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (Museu Nacional/UFRJ) received the skull of an adult woman, held at the Peabody Museum since 1870 following its transfer from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology. According to records, it was obtained by Walter Hunnewell, a Harvard graduate who accompanied the naturalist Louis Agassiz on an expedition to Brazil in 1865-66, serving as the mission’s photographer.

Recent findings suggest that the skull was described in the records as the “skull of a negro”, with an accompanying note stating it had been “exhumed in the streets of Rio de Janeiro”, although circumstances surrounding its removal are still under investigation. The remains may have been taken from the Cemitério dos Pretos Novos, a burial ground in Rio used for enslaved Africans who died after arriving in Brazil that operated in the 18th century and early 19th century. The burial ground was rediscovered in 1996 during construction work in the city’s port district.

It has been revealed that the Museu Nacional/UFRJ will assume temporary custody of the skull, which will not be publicly displayed nor used for research, reproduction or other purposes. Researchers will undertake further work to establish the woman’s origins before decisions are made about the skull’s final destination.

A ceremony on 11 November at the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro to mark repatriation of the remains of an enslaved woman from the Peabody Museum at Harvard University Courtesy Ministério das Relações Exteriores, Brazil.

“This return represents a historical responsibility for the museum,” Juliana Sayão, the deputy director of the Museu Nacional/UFRJ, said during the ceremony in Rio on 11 November. “We are confronted with the story of a person whose life was shaped by enslavement and the removal of her body from Brazil. Beyond assuming temporary custody, we are committed to treating this history with respect and responsibility.”.

According to recent reports, brazil’s minister of human rights and citizenship, Janine Mello, noted that the repatriation represents a milestone in acknowledging the historical violence resulting from enslavement. “The repatriation of human remains represents a fundamental step towards recognising the memory, history and dignity of the Black population of our country,” she said. “More than a century after they were taken from Brazil, these remains will return to the country to receive the dignified treatment to which they are entitled, in a process built on respect for memory, religious traditions and the communities involved.”.

Meanwhile, the Federal University of Bahia in Salvador received the remains of an enslaved African man of Nagô origin. The man is believed to have participated in the Malê Revolt in Salvador in January 1835, a major uprising led by both enslaved and freed Africans against slavery and religious persecution in Brazil. He was reportedly wounded during the uprising and subsequently died in hospital in Salvador.

A 2022 report on Harvard’s museum collections documented the presence of thousands of human remains, prompting scrutiny of how they had been collected and studied. Neither the museum nor the university returned The Art Newspaper’s requests for comment.

In a recent development, more than four million enslaved Africans disembarked in Brazil during the transatlantic slave trade, making it the largest destination for the forced migration of Africans across the Atlantic. The country was the last in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fine art photographer David Yarrow has sat down with Graham Bensinger for a long chat about his career and life.

It has been revealed that yarrow is one of the most commercially successful photographers working today. He’s probably best known for his dramatic, large-format black-and-white wildlife photographs, although he has moved into fashion, celebrity portraits, and staged scenes.

The Scottish photographer began his career in sports, covering the 1986 World Cup in Mexico for The Times of London, where he got a well-known shot of Diego Maradona holding the trophy aloft.

But as Yarrow tells Bensinger, he became disillusioned with sports photography after attending the Calgary Winter Olympics in 1988, fretting that it was too difficult to stand out from the many other photographers also covering events.

It has been revealed that so in his early 20s, Yarrow pivoted and moved into finance. On 9/11, he made some bold market moves minutes after the first plane hit the tower, netting him major bucks.

But Yarrow notes his finance career eventually fell apart when Bernie Madoff’s massive Ponzi scheme was uncovered, and investors pulled all their money out of his business.

If there’s one photo that put a rocket in Yarrow’s career, it’s the great white shark breaching while hunting a seal that he took off the coast of Cape Town, South Africa.

A post shared by David Yarrow Photography© (@davidyarrow).

Recent findings suggest that yarrow states he was with a picture agency at the time that sold it to newspapers and magazines around the world for him. It netted him roughly $16,000. The problem was Yarrow had spent $20,000 in the pursuit of that photo and so ultimately lost $4,000.

But redemption was on the way in the form of a Texas lawyer called “Jaws” who wanted to buy the great white photo. When Yarrow quoted $6,000, the lawyer couldn’t believe how cheap it was.

“That was my a-ha moment, or my road to Damascus moment, or when the penny dropped,” claims Yarrow. “That was when [I realized] one person could pay me more for a photograph than all of the newspapers and magazines in the world.”.

In a recent development, petaPixel covered Yarrow’s team portrait of the Norwegian soccer team on their way to the World Cup in the U.S. last summer. Yarrow got the team, which includes star striker Erling Haaland, to dress up in Viking gear.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American bathroom brand Kohler has created Dekoda, a health tracker specifically for the toilet, through its spin-off venture, Kohler Health.

Dekoda is designed to be discreet and intuitive, clipping to the side of the toilet bowl to give insights on gut health and hydration levels, and to detect the presence of blood.

In the emerging toilet-based health tracker market, it is the first device capable of blood detection, which it does through sensors developed at Kohler Health that identify haemoglobin.

The organization said the device is particularly useful for older individuals or those with chronic gut illnesses, who need to track their symptoms as part of their disease management programmes.

“When we developed Dekoda, our goal was to give people the tools to listen to their bodies, track meaningful results over time, and take charge of their own wellness journey,” said Kohler Health managing director Nora Tophof.

Industry observers note that “It’s important to realise that the human eye is only capable of seeing so much – and trace amounts of blood or other issues are not always apparent,” she continued. “Subtle biological markers, such as microscopic blood or early signs of dehydration, often go unnoticed.”.

“Dekoda works quietly behind the scenes to capture those crucial clues, giving people clear, objective data they can use to help shape behaviours or share with their doctor,” Tophof said.

People with dementia often forget to drink or lose the feeling of thirst, while people with gut diseases such as Crohn’s usually need to track their daily bowel symptoms.

A secondary target market is competitive athletes and fitness enthusiasts, who Kohler states can use the hydration data to make training adjustments.

Dekoda is compatible with most toilets. It has a simple flattened capsule shape in gleaming white polycarbonate and attaches to the outside of the rim with an adjustable clamp.

On the other side of the clamp, a customised camera points down into the bowl, using spectroscopy to detect the colour and consistency of urine and stool.

To withstand the bathroom environment, the exterior of the device is made of a polycarbonate that is antibacterial and chemical-resistant, while the mechanical components are made of stainless steel.

A specially trained algorithm analyses the collected data and insights are viewed in the accompanying Kohler Health app. It automatically tracks bathroom routines and identifies trends, while people can also add information about their meals, medications and exercise to add context, and share insights directly with their doctor when they desire.

Consumers’ data is encrypted as it travels between their devices and Kohler’s systems but decrypted and processed to provide the service.

Kohler Health said Dekoda, which was released in October 2025, is helping destigmatise the collection of gut health-related metrics, which individuals could previously only monitor through test strips or stool samples.

It is part of a small wave of latest devices focused on analysing the body’s fluids, from spit to menstrual blood, as wellness technology expands beyond watch-style heart rate monitors and activity trackers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The growing use of AI-generated food images in Japan, a country with strict laws against misleading product photography, is raising concerns.

Industry observers note that in much of the world, food photography on product packaging often exaggerates what is inside. But in Japan, it is illegal for companies to use misleading food photos on product packaging.

In Japan, food packaging must show the product exactly as it is even a tiny exaggeration is seen as misleading.

No fake ads. No chemicals. No adulteration. Just pure honesty in every bite. https://t.co/kFKP0n9a1c.

— Dr. Rajeshwari Iyer (@RajeshwariRW) October 28, 2025.

Industry observers note that japan enforces some of the world’s toughest packaging regulations. Companies must ensure that the photos on their packaging accurately reflect the actual product, and failing to do so can lead to legal consequences. Any discrepancy between a product’s image and the real item is considered misleading. Even minor exaggeration or embellishment can be treated as a violation.

According to recent reports, under Japanese law, photos on product packaging are treated as factual claims. If a photograph on a packet of crackers demonstrates toppings arranged in a certain way, the crackers inside must match that presentation. The size, shape, and appearance of the product should closely mirror what is depicted in the image.

However, despite Japan’s strict standards for product photography, AI-generated food images are rapidly spreading throughout the country’s food and restaurant industry, prompting a backlash from consumers, according to recent reports.

An increasing number of food and beverage businesses are turning to generative AI to produce food images, menus, and promotional posters. The practice has frustrated some Japanese consumers, who say they deliberately avoid visiting restaurants that use AI-generated promotional images.

It has been revealed that in one particularly example, a Japanese food truck went viral in the country after using AI images of a “tomato and scrambled egg rice bowl” that had a melted cheese pull look, despite the dish not having any cheese in it. Following online backlash, the food truck owner issued an apology and pledged to replace the AI images with real photographs.

Recent findings suggest that under current Japanese law, there is no requirement to disclose whether an image is AI-generated. However, in a country where the accuracy of product photography has long been subject to strict legal standards, the growing use of fake food imagery is raising questions about authenticity, consumer trust, and how far AI should be allowed to replace traditional photography and design.

Canva Now Lets Users Turn Off Generative AI Features

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Canva has introduced new settings that allow users to disable its generative AI features and reduce the amount of AI-generated material shown in its content library.
  • The generative AI setting disables a range of tools, including Magic Expand, Magic Write, Magic Design, Magic Layers, Magic Edit, Dream Lab, Canva Code, and AI Shapes.
  • However, the change does not disable every AI-powered feature on the platform.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Canva has introduced new settings that allow users to disable its generative AI features and reduce the amount of AI-generated material shown in its content library.

The generative AI setting disables a range of tools, including Magic Expand, Magic Write, Magic Design, Magic Layers, Magic Edit, Dream Lab, Canva Code, and AI Shapes. It also prevents consumers from generating images through Canva’s AI chatbot.

However, the change does not disable every AI-powered feature on the platform. Tools such as Background Remover and Magic Grab will remain available, even when generative AI is switched off. Canva says these tools will stay enabled because they “make everyday tasks faster without generating anything new.”.

The distinction is based on how the tools operate. While generative AI features create new content, Background Remover and Magic Grab work with existing images. The latter allows people to select an object within an image and reposition it elsewhere in the design.

Sources indicate that A second setting allows users to reduce the amount of AI-generated material displayed in Canva’s content library. When enabled, the platform will prioritise human-created templates, graphics, and other design elements in search results.

According to recent reports, however, the setting does not guarantee that AI-generated content will be excluded entirely. Canva claims that a “small portion” of its library consists of AI-generated material, and designs containing these elements will carry an AI label in their metadata.

In a recent development, both settings can be accessed through the profile menu. To disable generative AI tools, consumers should go to Profile, select Settings, open Permissions, and switch off Enable generative AI features. To reduce AI-generated content in search results, they can navigate to Profile, Your Account, and AI Personalization, then enable the option to show less AI content.

It’s no secret that AI has a popularity problem, and Canva appears to be listening to that sentiment. Last month, PetaPixel reported that the company released an image generation model that wasn’t trained on photographs.

Mecanoo transforms former gold vault into "city’s living room" in renovation of De Nederlandsche Bank in Amsterdam

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (732 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography is by Ossip van Duivenbode courtesy of De Nederlandsche Bank.
  • Dutch firm Mecanoo has completed a major renovation of the Netherlands’ central bank, which involved dismantling a 14-storey tower and opening up the former gold vault.
  • The Francine Houben-led architecture studio oversaw a complete retrofit of De Nederlandsche Bank, a 1968 structure that some had described as the nation’s ugliest building.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography is by Ossip van Duivenbode courtesy of De Nederlandsche Bank.

Dutch firm Mecanoo has completed a major renovation of the Netherlands’ central bank, which involved dismantling a 14-storey tower and opening up the former gold vault.

The Francine Houben-led architecture studio oversaw a complete retrofit of De Nederlandsche Bank, a 1968 structure that some had described as the nation’s ugliest building.

Located in the heart of Amsterdam, this huge concrete-slab building is in complete contrast to the city’s historic canal houses.

The original architect, Marius Frans Duintjer, had hoped to emulate the modernist works of Mies van der Rohe, but security requirements had resulted in “a fortress with fences, large boulders and armed military police,” according to Mecanoo.

The building was further complicated by later extensions, which included an extra storey above the low-rise main building and a cylindrical 14-storey tower built alongside the original central tower.

Mecanoo’s transformation was enabled by the relocation of gold reserves and banknote operations to a location in Zeist.

This allowed the architects to give the building a sense of transparency and openness that was envisioned from the outset, but had never been possible before now.

The project is an exemplar for sustainable renovation, as proven by its nomination for Dezeen Awards 2026.

Removing the cylindrical tower was pivotal, as it allowed space for a fresh public garden at the heart of the scheme.

This tower was carefully dismantled, allowing many materials to be reused.

Salvaged concrete was used to build a upcoming quay beside the canal, while the rest was donated to social housing projects in the city.

The removal enabled a reorganisation of the ground floor.

The entrance was relocated to Frederiksplein, while floorplates were cut away to reveal the 61-metre-long former vault, which has been transformed into an exhibition gallery.

“The most secretive part of the bank is now its most public,” remarked Mecanoo.

“Inside the vault, visitors can immerse themselves in exhibitions and interactive games that tell the story of gold, money, the economy and DNB’s core activities.”.

According to recent reports, the retained structures were newly clad in red ceramic bricks. These incorporate the brown tiles that clad the building previously, with the old tiles crushed for use as pigment.

These combine with new glazing, a Kastenfenster system of ventilated double-glazing with integrated sun shading, which has helped to reduce the building’s day-to-day energy requirements by an estimated 80 per cent.

Inside, the space linking the vault with the courtyard was designed as an indoor street, with seating areas along the edges and auditoriums (one formal, the other informal) at each end.

“Francine Houben’s inspiration came from the vibrant ‘street’ of the central hall in the former Faculty of Architecture building at TU Delft, which was destroyed by fire,” said Mecanoo.

The rest of the building is organised into zones with varying levels of security.

A five-storey atrium organises the semi-public area, which includes a meeting centre and a restaurant overlooking the Singelgracht, while the more secure employee zones are located in both the courtyard building and the tower.

The meeting centre occupies what was previously a double-height cash hall, with distinctive tree-like columns.

The original spiral staircase still stands, alongside a second added by Mecanoo, while custom-designed tables feature integrated lamps.

Timber was used for many of the latest surfaces, including a slatted ceiling made from locally felled poplar trees.

Shades of red, blue and orange extend across other surfaces and interior elements, including walls covered in recycled-plastic felt, carpets and furniture.

“The colour scheme is inspired by the vibrant paper currency from the last period of the Dutch guilder,” mentioned Mecanoo.

The interiors are completed by DNB’s collection of artwork, energy-efficient lighting systems and circular planting boxes.

“The renovation transforms De Nederlandsche Bank from a closed fortress into a transparent circular landmark, repurposing the former gold vault as the city’s living room for the public,” concluded Mecanoo.

Other recent projects by the firm include the rock-like Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, the tile-clad Villa BW and the book-inspired Macau Central Library.

Tech Report: Modigliani sculpture heads Phillips’s New York evening sale at $44.6m

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A striking limestone head by Amedeo Modigliani sold for $44.6m (with fees) at Phillips Modern and contemporary evening sale last night (17 November), leading a nearly sold-out auction totalling $85.75m ($104.4m with fees).
  • Robert Manley, Phillips’ chairman and worldwide head of Modern and contemporary art, remarked in a statement that there had been strong bidding across Modern, post-war and contemporary art: “Nearly 90% of the works offered had never been previously sold at auction, with many of the sale’s works coming from esteemed private collections where they had been for decades.
  • In a recent development, sales were brisk in a bustling room, the pace in part due to the large number of works backed by third party guarantees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A striking limestone head by Amedeo Modigliani sold for $44.6m (with fees) at Phillips Modern and contemporary evening sale last night (17 November), leading a nearly sold-out auction totalling $85.75m ($104.4m with fees). That is an increase of 55% from the same sale last November, which topped out at $54.8m ($67.3m with fees).

Robert Manley, Phillips’ chairman and worldwide head of Modern and contemporary art, remarked in a statement that there had been strong bidding across Modern, post-war and contemporary art: “Nearly 90% of the works offered had never been previously sold at auction, with many of the sale’s works coming from esteemed private collections where they had been for decades. Tonight’s results are a powerful reminder that truly exceptional works continue to inspire extraordinary competition in the market.”.

In a recent development, sales were brisk in a bustling room, the pace in part due to the large number of works backed by third party guarantees. With just 22 lots on offer—the house withdrew Derek Fordjour’s Haberdasher, estimated at $350,000 to $550,000, at the last minute—14 carried a guarantee.

It took less than a minute and a half, for instance, for auctioneer Henry Highley to hammer Claude Monet’s La Maison dans les roses (1925) at $3.2m, matching the $4m high estimate with fees.

Claude Monet's La Maison dans les roses.

On the other hand, the Modigliani, also guaranteed, sparked a ten-minute three-way battle, escalating from the starting bid of $18m to $28m in just a few seconds before slowing to $100,000 increments. A phone bidder speaking with Phillips specialist India Phillips ultimately prevailed over clients on the line with specialists Jeremiah Evarts and Kevie Yang, placing the winning bid at $38.2m ($44.6m with fees) on an estimate of $28m to $35m.

According to recent reports, the piece, dating from 1911 to 1912, is one of just 28 sculptures by the artist, and part of a larger series of limestone heads each titled Tête. The price, while impressive, failed to approach the $70.7m achieved by another work from the series at Sotheby’s Upcoming York in 2014, which remains the record for Modigliani sculptures. His painting record, $170.4m for the 1918 painting Nu couché—the sixth most expensive work ever to sell at auction—dates to the following year.

Recent findings suggest that the evening’s second-biggest lot was David Hockney’s eight-panel oil painting David, Celia, Stephen and Ian, London 1982, which sold for $10m ($12.2m with fees) within its $10m to $15m estimate. The artist, who died in June at the age of 88, made the work in 1982. It reflects his experiments at the time with photographing a subject from slightly different, overlapping viewpoints to create Cubist-inspired collages, and marks Hockney’s return to painting after a period focused on photography.

Helen Frankenthaler's Seabreeze.

The painting, which was sold by the Joel and Carole Bernstein family collection, also boasts an impressive museum pedigree, including appearances at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, and the National Portrait Gallery in London.

Rounding out the sale’s top three was Alexander Calder’s 1959 mobile Snow Flurry, May 14—one of the few works without a third-party guarantee, and being sold by the family of Brazilian art critic Mário Pedrosa. Yang caused some excitement when she raised her bid straight from $4.6m to $6m, a price no one else was willing to top. The total with fees was $7.5m, above a high estimate of $6m.

Helen Frankenthaler had the sale’s top result for a woman artist with Seabreeze (1980), which went for $4.5m (with fees). Frankenthaler followed that up a few lots later with Peacock Alley (1990) $2.7m (with fees), right in the middle of its $2m to $3m estimate.

The night’s only bought-in lot was Anselm Kiefer’s Melancholia (2005), which carried an estimate of $650,000 to $850,000, but bidding stalled out at just $500,000. The rust-coated painting features a polyhedral glass-and-iron sculpture mounted on the canvas.

David Hockney's David, Celia, Stephen, Ian, London August 1982 (Four Friends) (1982).

It has been revealed that and while Jackson Pollock’s 1946 abstraction Constellation did find a buyer, the work failed to meet its low estimate of $3.5m. Despite the current show of Pollock and his wife Lee Krasner uptown at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and a provenance boasting the legendary dealer Peggy Guggenheim, the work hammered at just $2.6m ($3.3m with fees). Frank Stella’s Port Tampa City, from the estate of the late dealer Robert Mnuchin, also hammered below estimate, at $2.8m ($3.5m with fees) despite an estimate of $3m to $5m. The orange canvas, in the shape of an eight-point star quilt block, dates to 1963.

According to recent reports, nevertheless, both paintings made the sale’s top ten list, slotting in at number eight for Stella and nine for Pollock, just above the second Frankenthaler. Other noteworthy results included Clyfford Still’s PH-589 (1959). Expected to sell for $4m to $6m, it hammered for $4.2m ($5.3m with fees) to an online bidder from Tel Aviv.

#45567. How Close Can an Arri-Powered Phone Get to an Alexa Cinema Camera?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1795 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Petapixel ↗ Open Full Page

How Close Can an Arri-Powered Phone Get to an Alexa Cinema Camera?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1795 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that that Honor and Arri are now partners is old news, but putting the latter’s Hollywood-style color science into a smartphone is the more intriguing proposition.
  • Recent findings suggest that the phone itself, the Magic9 Pro Max, features headline specs like a dual 200-megapixel camera system, a dedicated imaging chip, and a monster battery.
  • A full review focusing on still photography is forthcoming, but I visited Arri’s studio in Burbank, CA, in October 2026 to see how it helped shape the way the Magic9 Pro Max renders video.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that that Honor and Arri are now partners is old news, but putting the latter’s Hollywood-style color science into a smartphone is the more intriguing proposition. The Munich-based company seems like an unusual collaborator for Honor, the smallest of the five major Chinese phone brands.

Recent findings suggest that the phone itself, the Magic9 Pro Max, features headline specs like a dual 200-megapixel camera system, a dedicated imaging chip, and a monster battery. A more substantive addition is the phone’s Arri Cinema mode, inspired by Arri’s Alexa cinema cameras, which we’ve already seen in the Honor Robot Phone. This presents an entirely different way to capture video on Honor’s flagship.

A full review focusing on still photography is forthcoming, but I visited Arri’s studio in Burbank, CA, in October 2026 to see how it helped shape the way the Magic9 Pro Max renders video.

Arri’s history in analog cinema laid the foundation for its color expertise, though early on, the company essentially carried someone else’s color science since the film stock itself determined the look. Arri’s film scanner and film recorder, the Arri Scan and Arri Laser, became fixtures in studios, where engineers learned “what makes film look like film.”.

Moving to digital cameras enabled Arri to study many different film stocks to build a single default look, supported by a logarithmic brightness curve and a custom color gamut. Thus came the “digital negative,” a flat, data-rich image meant for grading rather than direct viewing.

With skin tones as a central design goal, the organization states it photographed many faces to build a gamut that could consistently render varied complexions. That also means more stable color science when footage is over- or underexposed, with shadows that don’t veer into purple territory. This reflects years of feedback from colorists on how swiftly they could achieve a finished look with Arri footage.

For Honor’s part, this marks a first in that it was one of the only Chinese phone brands (along with Huawei) that, until now, hadn’t partnered with a European imaging brand. While not terrible, its previous flagships couldn’t produce the kind of video quality competitors were delivering. Partnering with Arri isn’t just about catching up, but about ultimately surpassing every competitor, including the iPhone.

Honor handles the pipeline, which is why its own H1 chip is an integral hardware piece. That chip works in the RAW domain for what it calls “lossless noise reduction and extra dynamic range.” Achieving “cinema-grade” dynamic range requires capabilities beyond what a standard mobile processor offers, which is why this dedicated silicon works in tandem with Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset. Honor reps were coy about how this particular marriage actually works under the hood.

Recent findings suggest that what we do know is that Honor’s team in France worked closely with Arri in Munich, which helped tune the image signal processor (ISP) by sending weekly software revisions during development. Beyond that, Arri personnel made no contributions to the phone’s hardware design.

Here’s what Arri has to work with in the Honor Magic9 Pro Max: The dual 200-megapixel main (24mm equivalent) and telephoto (85mm equivalent) cameras both have CIPA 8-rated stabilization. Arri Cinema mode records up to 4K at 60fps, supports a 2.39:1 or 16:9 aspect ratio, and has a base Exposure Index of 160.

In a recent development, exposure Index (EI) is similar to ISO, though it functions differently on cinema cameras. Arri cameras normally work at the base setting for optimal dynamic range, which isn’t how it works on a smartphone camera given the smaller image sensors. The base EI is the setting where the camera’s designers determined the sensor captures a fixed range of light most effectively, delivering the best possible dynamic range. In practical terms, that means the phone needs more light to hit its sweet spot than an Alexa would, which makes sense for a much smaller sensor. Honor and Arri have to pull this off by warding off noise when shooting at higher EI settings in dim scenes.

Arri Cinema mode can shoot in LogC3, the logarithmic encoding used in Arri cameras before the Alexa 35, including colors that approach the LogC3 gamut. Honor claims both the main and telephoto cameras track the LogC3 curve almost perfectly, marking a first for Arri, which had never matched multiple sensors in a single device before. But there’s also a catch to exactly how this works.

Showing charts that compared the phone’s response against a real Arri camera, Arri indicates the phone clips in the highlights because its sensor isn’t custom-designed like Arri’s own “expensive” ones. The sensors are also vastly different in size, making the phone’s dynamic range far more software-driven than it would be on an Arri camera.

In a recent development, note that I only mentioned the main and telephoto cameras—because the Arri mode won’t work on the ultra-wide camera. Honor says it reluctantly left the lens out, citing vague time constraints since the partnership was only about six months old (at the time I visited). Rather than rush to get that out, it prefers to “get it right first” before committing to adding that lens. It’s just not clear whether that could happen through a software update or in a future device, since the main and telephoto cameras each required custom curves and color matching.

Recent findings suggest that my own take is that tuning a third camera may cost more money than time, and given that this is Arri’s first attempt without its own sensors, it leaves the ultra-wide as the odd lens out. Even so, a wider focal range isn’t unfamiliar territory for Arri, given that its Signature Prime line includes an 18mm lens, so we’ll have to wait and see.

Inside the Arri studio—on a newly built set with both an Alexa and a Magic9 Pro Max capturing the exact same scene—the side-by-side clips look surprisingly close.

Looking at the footage from both cameras later on my own computer monitor and on different phones or tablets, Arri’s clips offer better clarity and gradations in skin tones, but not by the margin I’d expect given how vastly different the two cameras are. It’s fair to say these results not only compete with the likes of Vivo and Oppo, but also fire a real warning shot at Apple. I’m no longer convinced the iPhone is the smartphone video king.

Recent findings suggest that both Arri and Honor point to how they shifted the phone’s color patches (open circles for where the phone started, solid for where it ended up) so its output lands near a real Arri camera. The default look matches Arri’s pre-Alexa 35 cameras, with 14 built-in LUTs that are always available in Arri Cinema mode out of the box.

Industry observers note that adding LUTs is easy, with a comically high 87 looks available directly from either Arri or Honor online, all assembled from the company’s Arri Media post-production house. These range from black-and-white variants that emphasize different color channels to period film emulations, seasonal grades, beauty, and teal-and-orange looks—all of which also work in DaVinci Resolve. Some are over-the-top throwbacks that might only fit very specific use cases.

While the sheer level of choice is undeniably substantial, it can swiftly become a mess once you bring them in. Assuming you add all 87, you have no way of rearranging, organizing, or deleting any. Before long, finding the one you’re looking for becomes an almost endless scroll. You can also freely import custom LUTs from other sources—including any LUT built with Arri’s color science—which only adds to the clutter. I pointed this out to Honor reps, who said they will see about fixing it.

Despite the potential for overcrowding the mode, Arri Cinema is a huge upgrade over what Honor had before. I’ve come away impressed not just by the image quality, but also by the versatility of the included LUTs, which make recording almost anything look interesting. Adding a film-like aesthetic that doesn’t feel like a papered-on filter is a factor, but so is shooting in Log with manual controls for creative license. Excellent stabilization and built-in audio controls help the cause. Tapping the microphone icon offers five directional options: Standard, Long-range, Close-up, Voice isolation, and Voice boost. They’re actually better than I expected, though you can still use an external mic if you want.

The mode offers 4K or 1080p at 24, 25, 30, 50, and 60fps. It also supports the APV 10-bit codec, which, despite some compatibility concerns, remains a viable ProRes alternative (thanks to smaller file sizes) when running those files through DaVinci Resolve.

Notably missing is 120fps, which is restricted to the standard Video mode and carries a dubious connection to Arri given the vague assurances I received. It’s not at all clear whether Arri’s color science is sprinkled in here, though my eyes tell me it’s not. What’s especially head-scratching is that the standard Video mode locks 4K resolution to the Vibrant style. Switch to any other style, and resolution drops to 1080p for reasons I can’t ascertain. A software update should easily fix that, but we’ll have to wait and see.

It’s important to remember a key distinction in defining Arri’s role, which is based on image science, not optics. Despite making lenses and accessories for its own cameras, Arri isn’t involved in what Honor is doing on the optical end at this stage. So, unlike Xiaomi and Leica, Vivo and Zeiss, or Oppo and Hasselblad—which routinely collaborate on lens hardware—that isn’t the case for the Magic9 Pro Max.

Sources indicate that at its core, a cinema organization teaming up with a phone maker is a commercial play. Arri reps note that cinema remains the company’s priority, even as the market for high-end cinematography shrinks amid falling competitor prices. Licensing Arri’s color science is a way to reach people who may never buy a cinema camera while making them familiar with Arri Looks and post-production workflows.

Arri tried this before by collaborating with Panasonic on software upgrades, including for the Lumix S1R II, GH7, and GH6, where Arri certified Panasonic’s implementation of the LogC3 curve. A smartphone partnership, however, is far more mainstream and exposes the brand to a much wider audience.

Sources indicate that I asked if we might see these color science changes apply to Honor’s still photography as well, but both brands were noncommittal. Arri reps admit they have little experience in stills but would like to see it happen, whereas Honor declined to discuss any roadmaps on that front. It’s not clear if the two brands signed a long-term agreement, but from the looks of it, they blueprint to collaborate on more than just a few devices.

Before comparing your balance to anyone else's, you need to know what the benchmarks actually include. Most retirement savings data from Vanguard, Fidelity, and the Federal Reserve covers:.

Sources indicate that what these numbers typically exclude: taxable brokerage accounts, real estate equity, HSA balances invested for retirement, pension values, and Social Security. For FI-minded savers, this distinction matters enormously — your total investable net worth is almost certainly larger than your "retirement savings" as defined by these surveys.

The gap between average and median retirement savings is one of the most key distinctions in personal finance. The average gets pulled upward by high-balance accounts — a single person with $5 million in their 401(k) dramatically inflates the average for their age group. The median (the middle number when all balances are ranked) gives you a far more honest picture of what a typical American actually has saved.

Industry observers note that notice how the gap widens with age. By 65+, the average is 3.3 times the median — meaning a small number of disciplined savers (or high earners) are pulling the average far above what most people actually have. The median tells you what a typical person in each age group actually holds. If you are above the median, you are doing better than half of Americans your age. But "better than average" and "on track for a secure retirement" are very different standards.

These numbers reflect defined-contribution initiative balances only — primarily 401(k) and 403(b) accounts.

Sources indicate that average balance: $13,265. Median balance: $5,400. Most savers in this bracket have been contributing for fewer than five years. The biggest advantage this group has is time — a 25-year-old contributing $6,000 per year with a 7% average return will accumulate over $1.2 million by age 65 without ever increasing their contribution. The FI community emphasizes that getting started early matters far more than starting with large contributions.

Average balance: $53,300. Median balance: $21,000. This is where employer matches start compounding meaningfully.
